questions.question: What permission settings are appropriate for an app that only checks balances using a read-only API key?

options.text: Allow only read access and disable trading and withdrawals
Publish the API secret key in a public repository
Enable every permission because reading requires them all

questions.explanation: Granting only the minimum necessary permissions reduces the possible damage if a key is exposed. Checking balances does not inherently require trading or withdrawal permission.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding exchange security and when its concepts apply

questions.question: What is the usual security purpose of a withdrawal-address allowlist?

options.text: To restrict withdrawals to addresses registered in advance
To hold the private keys of every external wallet
To create any coin without fees
To automatically delete exchange employees' accounts

questions.explanation: An allowlist makes it harder to send assets to unapproved addresses. Risk remains if an attacker also controls the process for adding new addresses, so it should be used alongside account protection.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding exchange security and when its concepts apply

questions.question: Why might withdrawals be suspended even when exchange and user logins are functioning normally?

options.text: Separate causes may exist, such as wallet maintenance or service liquidity problems
Successful login guarantees every withdrawal under consensus rules
Maintenance is impossible when a wallet app is installed

questions.explanation: Account accessibility and a service's ability to process withdrawals are different matters. Using a custodial service retains dependence on system operations and the counterparty.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding exchange security and when its concepts apply

questions.question: An address in your transaction history matches only the first and last few characters of an address you often use. What should you do before sending?

options.text: Compare the entire address again against the original receiving information you verified
Send as long as the first two characters match
Copy the address because it appears in recent history
Skip checking the tag if the address is long

questions.explanation: Address poisoning may try to make users copy a similar-looking address from transaction history. A match in a few characters is not evidence that it is the correct recipient.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding responses to wallet attacks and when they apply

questions.question: An unwanted token arrives in your wallet with instructions to sign on a particular website to claim a reward. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Assume it is completely safe because the token arrived
Enter your recovery phrase on the website to sign
Do not sign merely because you received the token; verify through official channels
Approve spending of all assets to receive a large reward

questions.explanation: Spam tokens or NFTs can advertise scam websites. Manually signing or granting an approval may introduce additional risk.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding responses to wallet attacks and when they apply

questions.question: What is a scam structure that allows token purchases but uses its contract to block ordinary users from selling commonly called?
questions.explanation: A honeypot token may contain malicious logic that attracts buyers and then prevents selling. Purchase activity in its trading history does not guarantee unrestricted withdrawals or sales.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding responses to wallet attacks and when they apply

questions.question: You only disconnect a website from your browser wallet. How should you treat ERC-20 spending approvals previously granted?

options.text: All approvals on every chain become zero immediately upon disconnection
Check whether the on-chain approvals need to be revoked separately

questions.explanation: Website connections and token spending approvals are managed in different places. Disconnecting may remove access to wallet account information, but it does not automatically revoke an existing on-chain allowance.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding responses to wallet attacks and when they apply

questions.question: What is the main risk of blind signing when a wallet asks you to sign data you cannot understand?

options.text: You lose the ability to use a block explorer
It is difficult to adequately verify the actual action you are authorizing
The recipient necessarily becomes an anonymous node
The signature always shrinks to 1 byte

questions.explanation: Blind signing includes approving data in a format that is difficult for a person to inspect. Even with a hardware wallet, authorizing something whose meaning you do not understand remains risky.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding responses to wallet attacks and when they apply

questions.question: Why is making your own recovery phrase by combining words from a famous song risky?

options.text: Phrases chosen by people are often predictable
Using words prevents an address from being created
A recovery phrase must be a person's real name

questions.explanation: Secure wallet creation requires sufficient randomness. Word combinations chosen for easy memorization can greatly reduce the set of candidates an attacker needs to search.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding responses to wallet attacks and when they apply

questions.question: A secondhand hardware wallet arrives with a recovery phrase already written on paper. What is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.text: Using the previous owner's phrase eliminates the need for a separate backup
An older phrase is always safer
A printed phrase has passed official verification
Someone else may know the phrase, so do not trust the existing wallet setup unchanged

questions.explanation: A seller or another person may have copied recovery information supplied in advance. Check that the device is in a trustworthy state and follow a verified procedure for generating new keys.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding responses to wallet attacks and when they apply

questions.question: What risk remains if you continue using an ordinary EOA whose private key may have been exposed?

options.text: The public address is automatically encrypted
The network automatically rejects every signature made by the attacker
An attacker with the same key can sign valid transactions
Changing the wallet app's name changes the key

questions.explanation: An ordinary key-based account cannot cryptographically distinguish different holders of a valid private key. Changing only the app password or account display name cannot invalidate an already exposed key.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding responses to wallet attacks and when they apply

questions.question: What is the purpose of reviewing a transaction simulation?

options.text: To regenerate a private key without a recovery phrase
To determine every future execution state conclusively
To inspect expected asset movements and execution results under the currently assumed state
To prove that any contract is free of bugs

questions.explanation: Simulation helps users understand expected behavior before signing. State changes before actual inclusion and limitations of the simulator mean it is not an absolute safety guarantee.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding responses to wallet attacks and when they apply

questions.question: Why separate a storage wallet from a small spending wallet when trying different dapps?

options.text: To make every transaction free of fees
To automatically duplicate the balances of both wallets
To limit how far approval and signing risks during testing can affect stored assets

questions.explanation: Separating keys and assets by purpose can limit how an incident in one environment spreads to other assets. Recovery information for the different wallets must also be protected independently.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding responses to wallet attacks and when they apply

questions.question: What is halved under Bitcoin's halving rule?

options.text: The existing BTC balances of all wallets
The newly issued subsidy allowed for a new block
The confirmation count of every payment

questions.explanation: The halving rule reduces the newly issued subsidy at specified block intervals. It does not halve existing holdings or directly set market prices.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding Bitcoin economics and when its concepts apply

questions.question: Besides the block subsidy, what revenue should be considered when calculating Bitcoin mining revenue?

options.text: Password usage fees from all wallets
All coins held in the previous block
Fees from the transactions included in that block

questions.explanation: Within the valid block-reward limit, miners can receive the new subsidy and fees from included transactions. Not all of a block reward is newly issued currency.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding Bitcoin economics and when its concepts apply

questions.question: What does hash rate measure?

options.text: The amount of personal information stored in a block
The number of decimal places in a token
The KRW value of one wallet
The number of hash computations performed per unit of time

questions.explanation: Hash rate measures the speed of hash computation, such as in mining. A high figure does not guarantee that a particular miner will find the next block.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding Bitcoin economics and when its concepts apply

questions.question: What arrangement combines work from multiple miners and distributes rewards under defined rules?
questions.explanation: A mining pool coordinates submitted hash work and distributes rewards. Distribution policies and dependence on the pool operator may vary by pool.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding Bitcoin economics and when its concepts apply

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes ASIC mining equipment?

options.text: It operates only if its owner's private key is made public
It always makes mining revenue exceed electricity costs
It combines every blockchain's consensus into one
It uses chips designed to perform a specific computational task efficiently

questions.explanation: An ASIC is an integrated circuit designed for a specific purpose. High computational efficiency does not guarantee profit after equipment costs, electricity prices, and difficulty are considered.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding Bitcoin economics and when its concepts apply

questions.question: Electricity prices rise while the amount of hash computation stays the same. All else equal, what is the direct effect on mining operations?

options.text: BTC in the wallet is automatically burned

questions.explanation: A higher price per unit of electricity raises the cost of the same amount of work. This factor in mining economics is separate from the protocol's subsidy rules.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding Bitcoin economics and when its concepts apply

questions.question: Which description best defines the Lightning Network?

options.text: An organization that fixes Bitcoin's price
A service that deletes Bitcoin's transaction history
A network that uses payment channels for Bitcoin payments
A rule that turns every transfer into a block subsidy

questions.explanation: Lightning processes Bitcoin payments using payment channels. Its requirements, including channel funding and routing, differ from direct on-chain transfers.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding Bitcoin scaling and when its concepts apply

questions.question: Why does a Lightning payment invoice include an expiration time?

options.text: Because all BTC is burned at that time
To forcibly close every channel at that time
To specify the period during which the invoice can validly be used

questions.explanation: A Lightning invoice may include an amount, receiving information, and expiration conditions. An expired invoice may need to be reissued; it does not mean BTC itself has an expiration date.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding Bitcoin scaling and when its concepts apply

questions.question: What network is used to test an app separately from mainnet assets that have real value?
questions.explanation: A testnet allows functionality to be tested without directly using assets on the live mainnet. Success on a testnet does not guarantee every mainnet security or performance condition.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding development networks and when they apply

questions.question: What is a developer-support service that distributes small amounts of test coins commonly called?
questions.explanation: A faucet helps developers obtain the test assets needed to send test transactions. Distributed test assets should not be treated as equivalent to real money.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding development networks and when they apply

questions.question: What is the symbol of Solana's native asset used for purposes such as paying fees?
questions.explanation: SOL is Solana's native asset. SOL differs from tokens separately issued on Solana, and arrangements may exist for another party to pay fees.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding major ecosystems and when their concepts apply

questions.question: Which address is important for identifying a specific token type among tokens on Solana?

options.text: A login address shared by every wallet
The IP address of the user's phone

questions.explanation: A mint account identifies a token type and manages information such as supply and decimal places. A matching name or symbol alone does not establish that two tokens are the same.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding major ecosystems and when their concepts apply

questions.question: Which statement best describes the XRP Ledger's basic consensus mechanism?

options.text: It stores transactions without validating them at all
It uses only SHA-256 proof-of-work mining like Bitcoin
A single central bank records every transaction
It uses a validator consensus process and does not use Bitcoin-style mining

questions.explanation: The XRP Ledger uses its own consensus protocol. Being a cryptocurrency does not mean every network uses the same mining mechanism as Bitcoin.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding major ecosystems and when their concepts apply

questions.question: Which protocol is known for communication between different chains in the Cosmos ecosystem?
questions.explanation: IBC is a protocol for transmitting and verifying packets between chains. Multiple chains do not connect automatically merely because they exist; supported implementations and connection configuration are required.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding major ecosystems and when their concepts apply

questions.question: What term describes chains connected to Polkadot's relay chain?
questions.explanation: A parachain is a chain that operates while connected to the relay chain in Polkadot's architecture. Each chain can have its own functionality and state.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding major ecosystems and when their concepts apply

questions.question: What is the name of the Cardano blockchain's native cryptocurrency?
questions.explanation: ADA is Cardano's native cryptocurrency. It should be distinguished from tokens on other networks to avoid confusing names or transfer networks.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding major ecosystems and when their concepts apply

questions.question: What is the main function Chainlink price feeds aim to provide?

options.text: Delivering external price information for use in smart contracts
Providing only interface backgrounds unrelated to blockchains
Buying every token at a fixed price
Issuing private keys on behalf of users

questions.explanation: Price feeds deliver external market data for on-chain applications to use. They do not guarantee a rise in any asset's price or trading profits.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding major ecosystems and when their concepts apply

questions.question: Which description most closely matches Filecoin's main use?

options.text: A network for providing and using distributed storage space
A system for publicly posting private keys
A service that instantly cancels transactions on every chain
A system that fixes a stock's daily closing price

questions.explanation: Filecoin is a distributed storage network with storage providers and users. Storage agreements and data-access conditions must be understood separately.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding major ecosystems and when their concepts apply

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes IPFS from a blockchain?

options.text: Every IPFS file is a coin traded on an exchange
An IPFS identifier always stays the same even when file contents change
Using IPFS eliminates the need for anyone to store the data
IPFS is a content-addressed file delivery and storage technology; it is not itself block consensus over all records

questions.explanation: IPFS identifies and delivers content. It can be used alongside a blockchain, but using IPFS does not itself imply blockchain consensus or permanent storage.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding major ecosystems and when their concepts apply

questions.question: Why does a naming service mainly connect names such as alice.eth to addresses?

options.text: To make a wallet's private key identical to its name string
To help people find blockchain addresses through readable names
To reach consensus on one address for every chain
To fix the price of ETH

questions.explanation: A naming service can link a long address to a human-readable name. The name's registration status and resolved address must also be checked for correctness.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding major ecosystems and when their concepts apply

questions.question: What is a significant deviation from USD 1 in the price of a dollar-targeting stablecoin called?
questions.explanation: Depegging occurs when the link between the target reference and market price weakens. Being designed for stability is different from always trading at the target price.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding stablecoins and when their concepts apply

questions.question: What is the process of returning a stablecoin to its issuer in exchange for the agreed underlying asset generally called?
questions.explanation: Redemption returns a token to the issuer or an agreed mechanism in exchange for the corresponding asset. Actual conditions, such as eligibility, minimum amounts, and processing times, must be checked.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding stablecoins and when their concepts apply

questions.question: Why can a Korean user holding a USD 1-targeting stablecoin not assume its value will always remain constant in Korean won?

options.text: The USD/KRW exchange rate can change
Receiving a token automatically issues Korean won
The US dollar has no exchange-rate concept

questions.explanation: Even if the price is stable against the dollar, the valuation in Korean won is affected by exchange rates. Stability against a reference currency differs from a fixed value in every currency.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding stablecoins and when their concepts apply

questions.question: What does a liquid staking token generally represent?

options.text: Only a fee receipt for a failed transaction
A shared private key for every exchange
A token representing deposited staking assets and associated rights
Central bank money that has not yet been issued

questions.explanation: A liquid staking token is designed to represent rights to underlying staked assets. Its price and actual redemption conditions depend on the protocol's structure and market conditions.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding staking and when its concepts apply

questions.question: Why might there be a waiting period after an unstaking request?

options.text: The protocol's exit process and the service's redemption procedures are required
Every chain operates only once a month

questions.explanation: Exiting staking is affected by factors such as active-validator management and redemption liquidity. Holding a token that can be sold does not mean the underlying asset can be redeemed immediately.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding staking and when its concepts apply

questions.question: Which label commonly indicates an annual simple-interest rate without reinvesting rewards?
questions.explanation: APR generally indicates an annual rate on a simple-interest basis. Check separately whether the displayed rate is fixed and which costs and reward assets it includes.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding yield displays and their assumptions

questions.question: What is the effect of redepositing rewards at the same rate to earn additional rewards called?
questions.explanation: Compounding occurs when earned rewards themselves begin generating rewards like principal. Even if the reward quantity grows, its valuation can decline if the reward asset's price falls.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding yield displays and their assumptions

questions.question: What should you check alongside a high yield figure on a staking or deposit screen?

options.text: Only the length of the wallet name
Only the color of the app icon
Reward sources, reward tokens, variable conditions, and risks of loss
Only the background photo on the sign-up screen

questions.explanation: Yield depends on reward sources and calculation assumptions. A rate displayed using newly issued token subsidies is not the same as sustainable cash income.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding DeFi operations and when their concepts apply

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a liquidity provider earning trading fees from someone simply holding tokens?

options.text: The LP's asset composition may change as swaps occur and prices move in the pool
The LP is always guaranteed the same token quantities
The LP is completely unaffected by falling token prices
The LP does not use smart contracts

questions.explanation: A liquidity provider's asset composition can change as the pool trades. Earning fees does not mean providing liquidity always outperforms simply holding the assets.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding DeFi operations and when their concepts apply

questions.question: What does liquidity mining generally mean?

options.text: Computing Bitcoin hashes using only a computer
Publishing private keys on the internet
Paying additional token rewards for activities such as providing liquidity

questions.explanation: Liquidity mining refers to token rewards designed to encourage DeFi participation. Despite the similar name, it works differently from Bitcoin proof-of-work mining.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding DeFi operations and when their concepts apply

questions.question: What does an NFT floor price usually represent?

options.text: A guaranteed redemption price for every NFT
A cost guarantee from the original issuer
The lowest asking price within the specified collection and market scope

questions.explanation: The floor price is generally the lowest listed selling price. It does not mean buyers will purchase every NFT at that price.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding NFT applications and when they apply

questions.question: How should a configured NFT royalty be interpreted?

options.text: It means NFT trades no longer incur gas fees
It specifies that part of resale proceeds should be allocated to creators or other recipients
The NFT holder receives all of the creator's copyrights
Payment is automatically guaranteed through every trading route

questions.explanation: Royalties concern the distribution of resale proceeds. A standard providing payment information must be distinguished from every marketplace actually enforcing payment.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding NFT applications and when they apply

questions.question: What problem may remain if you buy a game-item NFT and the game's servers later shut down?

options.text: The token may remain, but its in-game functionality may no longer be usable
The NFT automatically turns into cash
Your principal is guaranteed as soon as the game shuts down

questions.explanation: Token ownership records and provision of a game service are separate layers. Even if on-chain ownership remains, item functionality or access to content may stop.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding NFT applications and when they apply

questions.question: What is central to an NFT rental structure that grants another person only the right to use it for a set period?

options.text: Distinguishing the owner from the user and defining the usage period
Disclosing the private key to the other person
Permanently burning the NFT in every case
Making the owner impossible to identify

questions.explanation: A rental design can separate ownership from usage rights. Defining the usage period and permission scope in the contract allows behavior different from an ordinary ownership transfer.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding NFT applications and when they apply

questions.question: What risk particularly increases when a DAO treasury is controlled by only one person's private key?

options.text: Loss or theft of that key may affect the entire treasury

questions.explanation: Calling an organization a DAO does not automatically distribute operational authority. Check who can actually authorize spending and how the keys are held.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding DAOs and when their concepts apply

questions.question: What does quorum generally mean in a DAO vote?

options.text: The minimum participation requirement for a valid decision
The maximum size of a signature file

questions.explanation: A quorum is the minimum participation requirement for a voting outcome to be considered valid. It can apply separately from the condition that votes in favor exceed votes against.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding DAOs and when their concepts apply

questions.question: What mechanism requires waiting for a set period after an on-chain treasury spending proposal is approved before it can execute?
questions.explanation: A timelock adds a delay between approval and actual execution. It gives users time to inspect or respond to changes, but does not automatically identify malicious proposals.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding DAOs and when their concepts apply

questions.question: What is the usual purpose of delegating voting power?

options.text: To let another address exercise your voting power
To necessarily transfer both token ownership and the private key
To increase the token's total supply

questions.explanation: Voting delegation designates who exercises voting rights. Depending on the standard or implementation, it can be done without transferring token ownership.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding DAOs and when their concepts apply

questions.question: When reading a security audit report, what matters besides the audit firm's name?

options.text: Only the shape of the token price chart
The audited code version, scope, and unresolved findings
The color of the report's cover

questions.explanation: An audit reviews code at a specific point in time and within a specific scope. It does not automatically verify later upgrades or operational risks outside that scope.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding project evaluation and when its concepts apply

questions.question: What is most relevant to check when assessing rug-pull risk?

options.text: Whether wallet addresses are displayed in uppercase
Whether the token name is in English
Whether an administrator can unilaterally remove liquidity or assets
Whether NFT images are high resolution

questions.explanation: A rug pull includes situations in which operators remove funds or liquidity, betraying investors' or users' expectations. It is important to examine control over funds and the conditions for locking and unlocking them.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding project evaluation and when its concepts apply

questions.question: Applying a gas limit to a smart contract makes logical errors, such as incorrect calculations or access permissions, impossible.
questions.explanation: Gas limits resource usage. Whether a contract's business logic and permissions are correct must be reviewed separately.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing resource limits from code correctness

questions.question: Even if a wallet's recovery phrase has already been exposed, changing only the phone's screen-lock PIN blocks the attacker's access to the assets.
questions.explanation: An attacker can use the exposed phrase on their own device. Changing the phone lock cannot invalidate keys that have already been copied.
questions.learningObjective: The limits of changing local locks after seed exposure

questions.question: Even when the sender pays the fee to send ETH to an ordinary account, the recipient must submit a separate on-chain transaction just to receive it.
questions.explanation: Simply receiving ETH in an ordinary account does not require the recipient to submit a separate transaction. The sender's transaction updates the receiving account's balance.
questions.learningObjective: Gas obligations for an ordinary ETH recipient

questions.question: A successful coin-transfer status does not automatically prove that the seller shipped the promised physical goods.
questions.explanation: On-chain success and fulfillment of physical delivery are different matters. External facts require separate verification and data input.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing transaction success from physical fulfillment

questions.question: Two tokens with the same name and symbol must be the same asset even if their contract addresses differ.
questions.explanation: Names and symbols can be duplicated or imitated. Identifying an asset requires checking its network and contract.
questions.learningObjective: The difference between token names and asset identification

questions.question: A watch-only device with no keys can create an unsigned transaction and have a separate device holding the keys sign it.
questions.explanation: Preparing transaction contents can be separated from signing with a private key. The device without keys does not itself generate a valid signature.
questions.learningObjective: Creating unsigned transactions on a watch-only device

questions.question: Keeping ledger copies on multiple independent systems can reduce the risk of losing the entire ledger if one system's storage device fails.
questions.explanation: Distributed copies can improve resilience to the failure of a single storage device or location. Their actual effectiveness depends on deployment and operations.
questions.learningObjective: Replicated ledgers and the risk of losing a single copy

questions.question: Every database that replicates data across multiple servers automatically becomes a blockchain.
questions.explanation: Data replication alone does not create a blockchain. Design elements such as block structure, cryptographic links, and consensus must be distinguished.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing distributed databases from blockchains

questions.question: If the visible text is identical, the hash of the entire file must be identical even when its whitespace, encoding, or metadata differs.
questions.explanation: Hashing an entire file uses its actual bytes as input. Even when visible characters are the same, different byte representations or metadata can produce different results.
questions.learningObjective: The difference between displayed contents and byte contents

questions.question: Different blockchains may use different consensus mechanisms, and not every blockchain uses proof of work.
questions.explanation: Several consensus models exist, including proof of work and proof of stake. Different mechanisms may be used depending on participation permissions and trust relationships.
questions.learningObjective: The variety of consensus mechanisms

questions.question: A permissioned blockchain can restrict block production to approved participants while allowing the public to read its data.
questions.explanation: The permissioned classification does not necessarily mean that all read access is private. Access permissions can be defined separately for each role.
questions.learningObjective: Designing read access independently in permissioned networks

questions.question: Every stablecoin must use only US-dollar cash held in a bank as collateral.
questions.explanation: Stablecoins have different designs, including fiat-backed and cryptoasset-backed structures. The reference asset and the stabilization method must be distinguished.
questions.learningObjective: The variety of stabilization methods

questions.question: A Bitcoin wallet can use several UTXOs as inputs to one transaction to fund a single payment.
questions.explanation: A transaction can have multiple inputs. Several unspent outputs can be combined to cover the amount sent to a recipient and the fee.
questions.learningObjective: Funding a payment with multiple inputs

questions.question: Controlling a majority of the Bitcoin network's hash power allows the attacker to immediately calculate every other user's private key.
questions.explanation: A majority-hash-power attack concerns actions such as reorganizing the chain or double spending. It is separate from the ability to discover other users' signing keys.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing hash-power attacks from private-key theft

questions.question: Transactions from two different ordinary EOAs can use the same numeric nonce value.
questions.explanation: A transaction nonce is an account-specific counter. The same number in different accounts does not make their transactions identical.
questions.learningObjective: The account-specific independence of nonces

questions.question: A token's number of decimal places concerns amount display and unit interpretation, and is different from its market price.
questions.explanation: Block explorers treat a token's decimals and price as separate fields. More decimal places do not mean greater value.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing decimal places from price

questions.question: Simply hiding a token from a wallet app's token list does not remove its on-chain balance.
questions.explanation: Display settings and ledger state are separate. An actual change to token state requires a transaction under the applicable rules.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing hiding a display from changing token state

questions.question: In a Bitcoin transaction other than the special transaction that issues new coins, the difference between total input value and total output value is the fee.
questions.explanation: Input value not allocated to outputs in an ordinary transaction is treated as a fee. Total output value cannot exceed total input value.
questions.learningObjective: The input-output difference and transaction fees

questions.question: Creating multiple receiving addresses on the same Bitcoin network does not create a separate new blockchain for each address.
questions.explanation: Transactions involving multiple addresses are recorded on the same network ledger. Creating an address and creating a network are different tasks.
questions.learningObjective: Multiple addresses on a shared ledger

questions.question: A block explorer operator can cancel any completed transaction displayed on its website merely at a customer's request.
questions.explanation: An explorer displays transactions; it is not an administrator with arbitrary cancellation powers. An ordinary completed transfer requires a separate action, such as the recipient sending funds back.
questions.learningObjective: A lookup service's authority to modify the ledger

questions.question: If a photograph of a recovery phrase is automatically synced to the cloud, an online account breach could expose the phrase.
questions.explanation: Photo syncing can create an online copy of a recovery phrase. Recovery information must be protected with its storage locations and access routes in mind.
questions.learningObjective: Recovery-phrase screenshots and cloud exposure

questions.question: Using a hardware wallet makes every transaction safe even if you do not check the recipient address and authorization details displayed on the device.
questions.explanation: Even if a device protects the keys, a user can authorize a malicious transaction. Checking what is being signed remains necessary.
questions.learningObjective: Hardware wallets and mistaken approvals

questions.question: A previously spent Bitcoin output can validly be reused as an input to a new transaction as long as the recipient address is different.
questions.explanation: Reusing a spent output is double spending. Changing the recipient does not allow the same output to be reused.
questions.learningObjective: Restrictions on reusing spent outputs

questions.question: Devices performing Bitcoin proof of work use computing resources and electricity for repeated hash calculations.
questions.explanation: Proof of work requires computational work. It therefore consumes physical resources, including device processing capacity and electricity.
questions.learningObjective: The resource requirements of mining competition

questions.question: A smart contract that depends on particular external data may be affected if its oracle cannot provide new values.
questions.explanation: External data supply is also a service dependency. Handling stale or unavailable updates must be designed into contracts and operational processes.
questions.learningObjective: Oracle dependencies and service disruption

questions.question: Even if a seed-based wallet's device fails, its accounts can be restored in a compatible wallet if all required recovery information is intact.
questions.explanation: Asset state is on the ledger, and restoring the keys restores access. If an additional passphrase was used, it is also required.
questions.learningObjective: Recovery in a compatible wallet after device failure

questions.question: For a blockchain to function correctly, every node must receive a new block at exactly the same instant.
questions.explanation: Networks have propagation delays. Blockchain protocols are designed to transmit data and reach agreement on records in that environment.
questions.learningObjective: Propagation delays in distributed networks

questions.question: One Bitcoin transaction can create multiple outputs to split assets among different recipients.
questions.explanation: Bitcoin transactions support multiple outputs. This differs from double spending, which consumes the same output more than once.
questions.learningObjective: Multiple recipient outputs in one transaction

questions.question: When one block contains several transactions, all of those transactions share the same transaction hash as the block.
questions.explanation: Block hashes and transaction hashes identify different objects. Transactions in the same block each have their own transaction identifiers.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing block hashes from transaction hashes

questions.question: To increase a Bitcoin transaction's confirmation count, the recipient must repeatedly rebroadcast the same transaction.
questions.explanation: Confirmations increase as subsequent blocks are added after the block containing the transaction. They do not count how many times the recipient rebroadcasts it.
questions.learningObjective: Confirmation counts and subsequent blocks

questions.question: Even if one company controls every node and all operational authority, having many nodes means control is distributed among multiple independent parties.
questions.explanation: Distributing physical systems differs from distributing control. A single organization can control many servers.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing server counts from distributed control

questions.question: An app can check ownership of a particular NFT and use it as a condition for accessing content or a community.
questions.explanation: NFT ownership records can serve as a condition for access control. How access is actually granted depends on the app's design.
questions.learningObjective: Using NFT ownership as an access condition

questions.question: A smart contract can restrict a function so that only a designated administrator may execute it.
questions.explanation: Contract code can check the caller's address or permissions. A contract being public does not mean every function is available to everyone.
questions.learningObjective: Access control in contracts

questions.question: An ordinary Ethereum smart contract can wake up and change on-chain state by itself at a scheduled time without any related transaction or call.
questions.explanation: Rules can check a time condition, but actual execution requires a call originating from a transaction. Automation services also work by submitting execution transactions.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing elapsed time from transaction execution

questions.question: Possessing only a document's hash automatically authenticates who wrote the document.
questions.explanation: A hash acts as a fingerprint of data. Linking it to an author requires a signature or separately trusted registration information, for example.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing hashes from author authentication

questions.question: Gwei is a unit for expressing small amounts of ETH and is used to quote gas prices.
questions.explanation: Gwei is a denomination of ETH. It must be distinguished from gas, which measures resources.
questions.learningObjective: The unit relationship between gwei and ETH

questions.question: In a multisignature wallet requiring 2 of 3 distinct keys, signing twice with the same key satisfies the requirement.
questions.explanation: A 2-of-3 condition requires valid signatures from two distinct registered keys. Repeated signatures from the same key do not constitute approval by another key.
questions.learningObjective: The distinct-key requirement in multisignature wallets

questions.question: An ordinary transaction that sends existing bitcoin to another address is distinct from the process of issuing new bitcoin.
questions.explanation: Ordinary transactions spend existing spendable outputs. New issuance follows the block-reward rules defined by the protocol.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing asset transfers from new issuance

questions.question: If contract code differs from the developer's intention, the blockchain interprets the intention and automatically corrects the code before executing it.
questions.explanation: A contract executes according to its written code and inputs. Differences between intent and code must be found through development, review, and testing.
questions.learningObjective: The difference between developer intent and executable code

questions.question: Multiple token contracts created by different issuers can coexist on the same Ethereum network.
questions.explanation: Ethereum is a network that executes many contracts. Each token contract can be managed under its own address and rules.
questions.learningObjective: Multiple token contracts on one network

questions.question: Gas price and gas usage differ only in name and always have the same meaning and units.
questions.explanation: Gas usage measures resources, while gas price is the cost per unit of that resource. The two values are distinguished when calculating fees.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing gas price from gas usage

questions.question: Rather than trusting only a screenshot of a completed transfer sent by another person, it is appropriate to check your receiving address and the actual on-chain transaction status.
questions.explanation: A screenshot may be manipulated or show a different transaction. Check the recipient address, amount, and status of the public transaction.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing transfer screenshots from actual deposits

questions.question: Discussions about changing a blockchain's operating rules can be influenced by node operators and users as well as developers.
questions.explanation: Governance involves multiple stakeholders. The choices of participants who actually adopt and operate the rules are particularly important.
questions.learningObjective: Groups participating in governance

questions.question: Because Bitcoin records amounts in smaller units, amounts below 1 BTC can be held or transferred.
questions.explanation: Bitcoin uses subunits such as satoshis. Transactions do not have to use whole-number BTC amounts.
questions.learningObjective: Holding amounts below 1 BTC

questions.question: Once a game item is issued as an NFT, every other game immediately supports using that item.
questions.explanation: Being able to look up token ownership differs from a game supporting that asset. Support requires implementation for each game's features, formats, and operating rules.
questions.learningObjective: The limits of NFT support across apps

questions.question: Simply holding ETH in an ordinary wallet automatically makes you an active validator without any participation procedure.
questions.explanation: Validation requires steps such as the protocol's required deposit and activation, as well as running the relevant software. It differs from simply holding assets.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing asset ownership from validator participation

questions.question: To send or receive bitcoin, a user must first own mining equipment.
questions.explanation: Ordinary users can send and receive bitcoin through wallets. Mining is a separate role performed in the network.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing Bitcoin usage from mining equipment ownership

questions.question: Setting a lower gas limit automatically reduces the amount of computation needed for the same contract operation.
questions.explanation: The limit is the maximum allowed usage. If it is below the amount needed, execution may fail; the task itself does not become simpler.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing the gas limit from required computation

questions.question: Different NFTs identified by their NFT contracts and token IDs can refer to the same image file.
questions.explanation: NFT identity does not depend only on how different the images look. Token records can be separate even when they point to the same picture.
questions.learningObjective: The same image and different NFTs

questions.question: SHA-256 produces a 256-bit hash value for inputs it can process.
questions.explanation: SHA-256 has a fixed output length of 256 bits. This is independent of the size of the original file.
questions.learningObjective: SHA-256 output length

questions.question: Using an agreed shared ledger can reduce the work multiple companies spend repeatedly reconciling their separate transaction records.
questions.explanation: Shared records can help reduce the burden of identifying and reconciling discrepancies between separate ledgers.
questions.learningObjective: The cost of reconciling ledgers between companies

questions.question: Even if you lose a note containing a transaction hash, you can find the transaction again through the history of a related public address.
questions.explanation: The history of a public address may display related transactions. Losing a note does not delete the transaction record from the ledger.
questions.learningObjective: Finding transactions after losing a recorded identifier

questions.question: When a recipient returns coins sent by mistake, they generally do so by sending a separate return transaction.
questions.explanation: A new transfer in the opposite direction is made instead of erasing the original transaction. Whether funds are returned depends on factors such as the recipient's control and cooperation.
questions.learningObjective: Return transfers by recipients

questions.question: Every transaction submitted by pressing Send in a wallet must be included in a block, even if it has formatting errors or insufficient funds.
questions.explanation: Nodes check signatures and conditions concerning assets, formatting, and other requirements. Invalid transactions may be rejected during propagation or inclusion.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing pressing Send from valid transaction inclusion

questions.question: Using the same keys and account in two wallet apps creates new assets equal to the sum of the balances displayed in both apps.
questions.explanation: The two apps are simply viewing the same on-chain account. Increasing the number of display tools does not duplicate the actual assets.
questions.learningObjective: Using the same key in two apps

questions.question: A web address beginning with HTTPS guarantees that the website is the official wallet service you intended to visit.
questions.explanation: HTTPS concerns protection of the connection and does not automatically prove that a site genuinely belongs to a particular brand. Check the domain and official distribution channels separately.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing encrypted web connections from site authenticity

questions.question: One person can use multiple blockchain addresses or keys.
questions.explanation: People and addresses do not necessarily have a one-to-one relationship on a typical public blockchain. An address count therefore does not equal a count of people.
questions.learningObjective: The relationship between people and address counts

questions.question: Smart contracts can be used for nonfinancial information management, such as completion records, as well as asset exchange.
questions.explanation: A smart contract is a program that stores data and updates it according to rules. It does not necessarily have to include monetary transfers.
questions.learningObjective: Nonfinancial uses of smart contracts

questions.question: As more subsequent Bitcoin blocks accumulate, the work that must be redone to change an earlier block can also increase.
questions.explanation: Subsequent blocks reference the hashes of earlier blocks. Changing the past also requires satisfying the linked proof-of-work requirements again, increasing resistance to modification.
questions.learningObjective: Subsequent blocks and the cost of modification

questions.question: Even if a particular block explorer website is unavailable, the blockchain's transaction records may remain on other nodes.
questions.explanation: An explorer is a service that provides ledger data. Failure of that service and loss of the network's records are separate issues.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing explorer outages from blockchain failures

questions.question: A structure that stores and transmits transaction records across multiple nodes must also account for storage space and network resources.
questions.explanation: Distributed replication and validation involve data-storage, synchronization, and communication costs. Performance and operational resources should be assessed together when adopting the technology.
questions.learningObjective: Blockchain storage and communication costs

questions.question: A blockchain app cannot correct business information through a new transaction while retaining the existing transaction history.
questions.explanation: An app can retain its history while reflecting corrections through a new record or state-changing transaction. Preserving past records differs from changing current state.
questions.learningObjective: Correction records that retain history

questions.question: Reading records in a block explorer without submitting an on-chain state-changing transaction does not incur protocol gas fees for that lookup.
questions.explanation: Reading recorded data differs from executing a state-changing transaction. Any fee charged by a lookup service itself is separate from protocol gas fees.
questions.learningObjective: Read-only lookups and protocol fees

questions.question: A smart contract call that transfers 0 ETH incurs no gas fee even if it changes contract state.
questions.explanation: Contract execution uses resources even when no ETH is transferred. A state-changing transaction can incur execution costs.
questions.learningObjective: Zero ETH transferred and resource costs

questions.question: Issuing an NFT always stores the entire linked original image and video files inside the blockchain.
questions.explanation: An NFT may use links or metadata pointing to external files. The token record must be distinguished from the storage location of its linked media.
questions.learningObjective: The variety of NFT media storage locations

questions.question: Because proof of stake is not proof of work, its node computers and network communications use no electricity at all.
questions.explanation: Proof of stake still uses computers for validation, communication, and storage. Different energy-use characteristics from proof of work do not mean zero electricity usage.
questions.learningObjective: Proof of stake and resource consumption

questions.question: Enterprise permissioned blockchains cannot use smart contracts.
questions.explanation: Permissioned platforms such as Hyperledger Fabric also support smart contracts. Permissioning and support for contract execution are separate characteristics.
questions.learningObjective: Smart contract support in permissioned networks

questions.question: Nodes following the same consensus rules do not necessarily need to use computers from the same manufacturer.
questions.explanation: Consensus concerns the rules for determining valid records. Nodes can have different hardware and network configurations.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing consensus rules from identical equipment

questions.question: When a Bitcoin miner finds a block, that miner automatically receives the right to produce the next block as well.
questions.explanation: Finding the next block requires competing again. Previous success alone does not guarantee the next success.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing previous mining success from the next production right

questions.question: If a block's number is 500, it contains exactly 500 transactions.
questions.explanation: The block number indicates its position in the chain. Its transaction count is separate information.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing block numbers from transaction counts

questions.question: A permissioned network can have procedures for revoking permissions when participants leave or violate rules, in addition to participant approval procedures.
questions.explanation: A structure that manages participation permissions can operate rules for registration and removal. Specific policies depend on network governance.
questions.learningObjective: Granting and revoking permissions

questions.question: Issuing a new token on Ethereum always requires building a separate new blockchain for that token.
questions.explanation: Tokens can be created by deploying contracts on the existing Ethereum network. Token issuance and building a new network are separate tasks.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing token creation from building an independent network

questions.question: Reusing a custodial asset-service password on another website can allow a breach of that website to lead to an attack on the asset account.
questions.explanation: Damage can spread if an exposed password also works on other services. Unique passwords for each service and additional authentication can help.
questions.learningObjective: Risks of reusing service passwords

questions.question: For a hash function with a fixed output length, different inputs producing the same hash value are theoretically possible.
questions.explanation: Collisions theoretically exist because the number of outputs is finite relative to the possible inputs. Secure hash functions are designed to make finding a collision practically difficult.
questions.learningObjective: The theoretical possibility of hash collisions

questions.question: Even when a smart contract reads its own stored variable, an external oracle must provide that value again.
questions.explanation: A contract can directly use its own on-chain state. An external oracle provides a route for connecting data from outside the chain.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing on-chain data from external data

questions.question: If you lose the private key and all recovery information for an ordinary key-based wallet with no separate recovery mechanism, the protocol reissues a spending key when you submit only the public address.
questions.explanation: A public address cannot reissue the authority to spend assets. Ordinary key-based wallets require preservation of the necessary keys or recovery information.
questions.learningObjective: The limits of key loss without an additional recovery mechanism

questions.question: An app that uses blockchain does not need protection against ordinary security threats such as malware and phishing.
questions.explanation: Blockchain does not protect users' devices or websites from every threat. Key management and ordinary cybersecurity measures remain necessary.
questions.learningObjective: The relationship between blockchain and general security measures

questions.question: A token whose issuance and redemption are managed by a company can still be designed to transfer on a public blockchain.
questions.explanation: The openness of the underlying network and the management structure for token issuance and redemption are different matters. Issuer dependence can exist on a public chain.
questions.learningObjective: Public ledgers and issuer control can coexist

questions.question: Propagation delays and similar factors can temporarily cause different candidate blocks at the same height to be known on Bitcoin.
questions.explanation: A temporary fork can occur when several miners find blocks at similar times. Chain-selection rules subsequently resolve it.
questions.learningObjective: Temporary competing blocks

questions.question: Once a service is deployed on a blockchain, it will always remain fully usable even if operating nodes and maintenance disappear.
questions.explanation: A blockchain also requires operating nodes and software. Weaker network maintenance can affect availability and security.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing distributed ledgers from guaranteed permanent service

questions.question: If a Bitcoin miner creates a reward larger than the rules allow, other validating nodes can reject the block.
questions.explanation: Miners must also follow issuance and transaction-validation rules. Completing proof of work does not permit arbitrary issuance.
questions.learningObjective: Validating excessive issuance rewards

questions.question: For an ordinary ETH transfer where you pay your own fees, you must consider the balance needed for gas as well as the transfer amount.
questions.explanation: The ETH being sent and the execution fee are separate costs. Check that sufficient assets are available for the transaction to be processed validly.
questions.learningObjective: Transfer balances and funds for fees

questions.question: Verifying only a transaction signature on a public blockchain always reveals the sender's real name and physical address.
questions.explanation: Signature verification checks the relationship between a transaction and a key. Linking it to a real identity requires separate registration or external information.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing signatures from real-world identity authentication

questions.question: Everyone who wants to use Bitcoin must first download the entire blockchain to their phone.
questions.explanation: Lightweight wallets that do not download the whole chain are available. Running a full validating node differs from ordinary wallet usage.
questions.learningObjective: The availability of lightweight wallets

questions.question: Even if a dapp's web-interface server stops operating, its deployed smart contract may remain on the blockchain.
questions.explanation: The user interface and contract execution environment may be separate components. A website outage does not necessarily delete the contract itself.
questions.learningObjective: Separating web interfaces from deployed contracts

questions.question: Sending a token on Ethereum does not necessarily mean that protocol fees are paid in that same token.
questions.explanation: ETH is the native gas-fee asset on Ethereum mainnet. The token being sent must be distinguished from the asset used for network fees.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing transferred tokens from fee assets

questions.question: An ordinary Bitcoin transaction is valid even when its outputs exceed its inputs, as long as the recipient agrees.
questions.explanation: Except for the special transaction that creates new issuance, output value cannot exceed input value. The recipient's agreement does not change this rule.
questions.learningObjective: Input-value limits in ordinary transactions

questions.question: A coinbase transaction in the Bitcoin protocol is a customer transfer that only the Coinbase exchange can create.
questions.explanation: Coinbase transaction is the term for the special transaction through which a miner receives a block reward. It is distinct from the exchange with the same name.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing coinbase transactions from the exchange name

questions.question: Approving a contract to spend tokens is different from disclosing the private key itself to that contract.
questions.explanation: A spending approval specifies which token permissions a contract receives. Dangerous permissions can be granted without disclosing the private key, so approval details must be checked.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing token spending permissions from private-key disclosure

questions.question: A hard fork always results in two chains operating permanently, regardless of participants' choices.
questions.explanation: A hard fork is an incompatible rule change. Whether separate chains continue to operate depends on whether participants support and run each set of rules.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing hard forks from permanent chain separation

questions.question: Publishing a smart contract's code is enough to establish that it contains no exploitable errors.
questions.explanation: Publication enables review but does not guarantee correctness. Public code can still contain vulnerabilities.
questions.learningObjective: The security limits of public code

questions.question: Adding a digital signature to a public transaction automatically encrypts its contents so that others cannot read them.
questions.explanation: Digital signatures and encryption serve different purposes. The contents of a signed transaction can still be viewed if it is recorded on a public ledger.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing signing from confidentiality

questions.question: Knowing a transaction hash lets you view the original private key that signed the transaction in a block explorer.
questions.explanation: A transaction hash is an identifier for public lookup. Providing a private key to an explorer or recording it on a public ledger is not part of a normal signing process.
questions.learningObjective: The public nature of transaction hashes

questions.question: After reconnecting, a temporarily disconnected node can obtain missed records from other nodes and validate them.
questions.explanation: Through synchronization, a node obtains and validates blocks and other data it does not yet have. A disconnection does not permanently prevent participation.
questions.learningObjective: Synchronization of reconnected nodes

questions.question: Even when a transaction's signature is valid, its balance, spending conditions, and other requirements must also be checked against the rules.
questions.explanation: A signature is one element used to verify authorization. Other validity rules, such as available assets and contract conditions, must also be satisfied.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing signature validity from transaction conditions

questions.question: On Ethereum, the burned base-fee portion is distinct from the tip paid to validators.
questions.explanation: The base fee is burned, while the priority fee acts as a tip. Not all gas fees become validator revenue.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing base-fee burning from fee payments

questions.question: Operating a Bitcoin full node necessarily requires that node to participate in mining.
questions.explanation: A full node that validates and relays transactions and blocks can operate without mining. Not every full node is a block producer.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing full nodes from mining participation

questions.question: Deleting a self-custody wallet app from a phone automatically deletes the on-chain balance of its address.
questions.explanation: Deleting the app affects local software and data. However, losing the key backups as well may remove access even though the assets remain on the ledger.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing app deletion from on-chain state

questions.question: If you know a Bitcoin receiving address, you can send to it even when the recipient's wallet app is closed.
questions.explanation: Receiving bitcoin occurs through transaction records on the ledger, rather than by delivering a file to the wallet app. The recipient can open the wallet later to check the state.
questions.learningObjective: The recipient's online status

questions.question: The To field of an Ethereum transaction is always a person's ordinary account and can never be a smart contract address.
questions.explanation: A transaction's recipient can be an ordinary account or a smart contract. Targeting a contract can execute its functionality.
questions.learningObjective: Types of transaction recipients

questions.question: A circulating market capitalization of KRW 1 trillion means the issuer holds KRW 1 trillion in cash in a separate account.
questions.explanation: Circulating market capitalization is a valuation metric calculated by multiplying price by circulating supply. It does not directly show cash reserves or redemption claims available to all holders.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about market metrics and explaining why

questions.question: A Solana wallet can display balances of SOL and multiple separately issued tokens together.
questions.explanation: One wallet interface can look up several types of on-chain assets. Each token's identifying information, such as its mint address, must be distinguished.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about Solana and explaining why

questions.question: If an RPC provider temporarily stops operating, an app may be unable to read balances even though the entire blockchain has not stopped.
questions.explanation: RPC provides a connection point through which an app accesses a chain. An outage at that provider must be distinguished from the consensus status of the underlying network.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about app architecture and explaining why

questions.question: If an address looks identical on testnet and mainnet, its test-coin balance can automatically be used on mainnet.
questions.explanation: Each network maintains separate state and balances. Identical address formatting does not automatically convert test assets into mainnet assets.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about test environments and explaining why

questions.question: Even if adding mining equipment increases hash rate, actual rewards remain affected by factors such as network difficulty and electricity costs.
questions.explanation: Processing speed alone cannot determine net profit. Overall competition, asset prices, equipment costs, and operating costs must be considered together.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about mining economics and explaining why

questions.question: The leverage multiple offered by an exchange affects sensitivity to losses as well as gains.
questions.explanation: Leverage creates large price exposure relative to equity. Even a small unfavorable price movement can bring margin exhaustion or liquidation closer.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about market risk and explaining why

questions.question: Because an airdropped token was free, it cannot cause asset losses during approval or exchange.
questions.explanation: Even with zero acquisition cost, risks include signing on scam websites, malicious approvals, and transaction fees. Receiving a token and using it safely are separate matters.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about token distribution and explaining why

questions.question: High TVL alone proves both a protocol's annual net profit and protection of users' principal.
questions.explanation: TVL is a metric related to deposited value. It does not directly prove protocol profit, contract safety, or guaranteed redemption.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about DeFi risks and explaining why

questions.question: Splitting holdings between two stablecoins can still leave common risks if both depend on the same reserve assets or service.
questions.explanation: Assets with different names can share the same causes of failure. Diversification should be assessed through reserves, custodians, and connecting structures, not only the number of tokens.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about market risk and explaining why

questions.question: A faucet distributing test coins can send tokens only if it receives the user's mainnet recovery phrase.
questions.explanation: Ordinary receipt requires only a public address, not a private key or recovery phrase. Be wary of requests for secret information under the pretext of providing testing support.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about test environments and explaining why

questions.question: A product that redeploys deposited assets into another protocol can also be affected by risks in that other protocol.
questions.explanation: Linking multiple contracts can connect the impact of failures as well as functionality. Reviewing only the visible app can make it difficult to understand all dependencies.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about DeFi risks and explaining why

questions.question: Exchange login credentials and a blockchain wallet's recovery phrase are different authentication and recovery mechanisms.
questions.explanation: A custodial service account follows the service's login system, while a self-custody wallet manages keys. Information for one should not be entered as though it were the other's official recovery method.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about account security and explaining why

questions.question: Joining a mining pool can provide access to a reward-distribution method intended to reduce variability in payouts.
questions.explanation: Combining work from multiple participants and sharing rewards can spread payouts compared with mining individually. Specific payment rules and operator risks differ by pool.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about mining economics and explaining why

questions.question: Even if anyone can view the image represented by an NFT, a separate on-chain ownership record for that token can still exist.
questions.explanation: Access to content and token ownership records are different matters. The ability for anyone to view a file should not be treated as the same as owning the token.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about NFTs and explaining why

questions.question: Every Solana token must use the same name, and tokens cannot be distinguished by mint address.
questions.explanation: Different mint accounts can represent different token types. Checking the mint identifier rather than relying on a name or symbol is important.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about Solana and explaining why

questions.question: The asset paid as a staking reward can differ from the currency in which you measure returns.
questions.explanation: Rewards may be paid in tokens while a user values them in Korean won or dollars. Token prices and exchange-rate changes affect the measured return.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about staking and explaining why

questions.question: The number of tokens used for voting and the actual voting participation rate are different metrics.
questions.explanation: Participation relates to how much of the total eligible voting power is actually exercised. Having many token holders does not mean all of them participate in every proposal.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about DAO operations and explaining why

questions.question: Even with the same staking reward rate, different operator fees can lead to different net rewards for users.
questions.explanation: Check whether the advertised rate is gross or net of costs. Operator fees and other expenses can reduce the amount received.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about staking and explaining why

questions.question: If a token's logo displays correctly in an app, the technical possibility that it is a fake contract imitating the same symbol is eliminated.
questions.explanation: A logo or symbol cannot replace authenticity checks. Verify identifying information such as the supported network and official contract address.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about app architecture and explaining why

questions.question: An exchange can distinguish multiple deposits from the same customer using one shared address and different identifying tags.
questions.explanation: Some networks and services use a tag or memo in addition to an address. Check both types of information required by the receiving service.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about deposit and withdrawal practices and explaining why

questions.question: A product with zero trading fees always has zero costs from the spread or price impact as well.
questions.explanation: Explicit trading fees and costs arising from execution prices are different. Spreads or slippage may cause execution at a less favorable price than expected.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about market trading and explaining why

questions.question: Holding 10 different cryptocurrencies means the entire portfolio can never decline at the same time.
questions.explanation: Multiple assets can react together to the same market shock. A large number of holdings does not eliminate correlation or the risk of loss.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about market risk and explaining why

questions.question: Tokens issued on the XRP Ledger and XRP itself are distinct assets.
questions.explanation: XRP is the ledger's native asset, while issued tokens are separate assets with conditions related to their issuers and other factors. Being on the same ledger does not give them identical rights.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about the XRP Ledger and explaining why

questions.question: Two chains using an IBC connection still have distinct chain states and operating rules.
questions.explanation: Interoperability verifies and delivers messages between chains. Connecting them does not merge all state and operational authority into one.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about interoperability and explaining why

questions.question: Airdrop eligibility can be determined using the state of addresses at a particular point in time.
questions.explanation: A snapshot records holdings or participation at a specified time as a basis for distribution. Actual eligibility conditions vary by project.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about token distribution and explaining why

questions.question: All resting orders visible in an order book are irrevocable and therefore establish future trading volume.
questions.explanation: Resting orders can be changed or canceled before execution. Currently displayed depth should not be treated as liquidity guaranteed to remain in the future.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about market trading and explaining why

questions.question: Even if a Lightning channel has enough total capacity, a payment may be difficult if its balance in the required direction is insufficient.
questions.explanation: Channel funds serve different roles depending on which side can send to the other. Total capacity must be distinguished from the amount payable in a particular direction.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about Lightning and explaining why

questions.question: The risk of a hardware wallet device failing and the risk of losing its recovery information at the same time should be managed separately.
questions.explanation: It may be possible to restore keys using a compatible device and recovery information. Storage arrangements should also consider losing both the device and the backup together.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about wallet usage and explaining why

questions.question: Selling coins and seeing a KRW balance on an exchange is a separate step from withdrawing that KRW to a bank account.
questions.explanation: Trading changes the composition of assets held within the service. Payment to an external bank account requires a separate withdrawal request and processing procedure.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about deposit and withdrawal practices and explaining why

questions.question: A limit order can remain partly or entirely unfilled if its price condition is not met or there is insufficient opposing volume.
questions.explanation: A limit order restricts the prices at which execution is allowed. Setting a price condition differs from guaranteeing execution of the desired quantity.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about market trading and explaining why

questions.question: If XRP is sent without a tag to an exchange that requires one, the protocol automatically finds the customer's name and always credits the deposit.
questions.explanation: The network does not automatically know how an exchange identifies customers internally. A missing tag may require manual verification or a recovery procedure by the service.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about deposit and withdrawal practices and explaining why

questions.question: A large project community means you can skip reviewing operator permissions and fund-management practices.
questions.explanation: Community size and technical safety are different factors. Membership counts may be inflated, and actual contract permissions and asset-control structures must be checked.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluating statements about user protection and explaining why

questions.question: Holding 1 DAO token always grants the same one-person-one-vote power in every DAO.
