questions.explanation: EIP-712 does not by itself complete replay protection. The contract must verify one-time conditions such as a nonce and update their used state.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding the application's responsibility for replay protection

questions.question: Why does EIP-155 include a chain ID in legacy Ethereum transaction signatures?

options.text: To reduce replay attacks using signed transactions on other chains
To let different accounts share the same transaction nonce
To process every transaction of an account with one signature
To replace sender transaction-order checks with chain-ID checks

questions.explanation: Including the chain ID in the signed data distinguishes transaction contexts across chains. Transaction ordering within an account is governed by separate nonce rules.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding the scope of EIP-155 protection

questions.question: A recovery phrase passes its BIP-39 checksum check. What is not guaranteed by that fact alone?

options.text: Some input errors have been structurally checked
The phrase is the backup of the wallet the user originally used
The phrase can be used in the seed-generation procedure
The phrase satisfies the prescribed checksum structure

questions.explanation: A checksum checks format and some input errors. It does not establish who created the phrase or whether it corresponds to the desired wallet.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding recovery-phrase checksum limitations

questions.question: An online shop publicly exposes an extended public key it received for generating payment addresses. Apart from direct spending authority, what concern arises?

options.text: An exposed extended public key can reveal only one address
Without a private key, relationships between multiple addresses cannot be inferred
Multiple derivable addresses and their transactions may be linked
Even an extended-public-key holder cannot link newly generated child addresses

questions.explanation: An extended public key can derive many child public keys, potentially revealing a group of related addresses. This is a privacy issue distinct from private-key exposure.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding privacy risks from extended public-key exposure

questions.question: A transaction setting a malicious spender's ERC-20 allowance to 0 is confirmed. Which statement correctly describes its effect?

options.text: It restricts new allowance-based spending but does not reverse completed transfers
It retroactively cancels every past transfer by that spender
It also revokes other users' approvals for the same spender
Revocation takes effect only after moving the account to a new owner address

questions.explanation: Revocation applies to subsequent actions using the allowance. It does not retroactively cancel transactions already validly completed.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding when approval revocation takes effect

questions.question: A browser wallet emits the EIP-1193 accountsChanged event. What should an app update?

options.text: Only the old account address that will be used for the next signing request
Only the chain ID while retaining the account address
Balances, permissions, and display state for the selected account
Only the display name while retaining the previous account's balances

questions.explanation: A change in the connected account changes the app's address and authorization context. The app must not keep displaying the old account's state or use it in signing requests.
questions.learningObjective: Handling wallet account-change events

questions.question: You change the bytes of a file stored using the same IPFS import settings. What generally happens to its identifier?

options.text: The CID is a storage-server address and is independent of content
The original CID always remains unchanged if the filename is unchanged
The existing CID automatically changes to refer to the new content
A different CID is generated for the modified content

questions.explanation: A CID is based on content and its encoding structure. With the same settings, changing the content generally changes the CID.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding content edits and CID changes

questions.question: To expect the same CID when adding the same file to different IPFS nodes, what else must match?

options.text: Only the gateway host and folder name instead of the content
Import settings that determine content structure, such as chunking and codecs
Only the filename and local path instead of the content
Only the upload time and runtime instead of import settings

questions.explanation: Even identical bytes can yield different content graphs and CID representations when chunking or codec choices differ. Comparisons assume matching content and settings.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding prerequisites for comparing CIDs of identical content

questions.question: An app wants to improve the continued availability of an IPFS image. Which operational measure is appropriate?

options.text: Pin the content on a continuously operating node or service
Treat a gateway's temporary cache as completed permanent storage
Assume one retrieval makes every node store it permanently
Record only the CID on-chain, then delete the original and all copies

questions.explanation: Pinning keeps a node from removing the content through garbage collection. Long-term access requires ongoing storage and serving of the actual data.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding pinning and long-term serving responsibility

questions.question: What is the main purpose of verifying content returned by an IPFS gateway against the requested CID?

options.text: Determine that it is the application's newest version
Check that the received data matches the requested content identifier
Determine that enough copies are stored on other nodes
Determine that the responding provider is the file's original author

questions.explanation: Content-address verification checks the integrity of bytes and the content graph. Truthfulness and freshness of the content are separate issues.
questions.learningObjective: Verifying content integrity in gateway responses

questions.question: A confidential document must be stored on the public IPFS network. What is an appropriate basic design for confidentiality?

options.text: Replace access control with the assumption that the CID is hard to guess
Assume stored plaintext is secret when node-to-node connections are encrypted
Assume login protection on one gateway protects every IPFS copy
Encrypt before uploading and manage decryption keys separately

questions.explanation: Encryption between nodes differs from encrypting the file itself. Protecting confidential content on a public network requires content encryption and key management.
questions.learningObjective: Handling confidential data in public storage

questions.question: A Fabric endorsement policy is AND(Org1, Org2). Only endorsements from two different peers belonging to Org1 have been collected. What is the result?

options.text: The policy is not satisfied because an Org2 endorsement is also required
The ordering service automatically generates the missing organization's endorsement
Two peers in one organization automatically substitute for Org2
Two endorsement signatures satisfy the policy

questions.explanation: An AND policy requiring organizations must satisfy each specified organization's requirement. More signatures from the same organization cannot replace another organization's requirement.
questions.learningObjective: Assessing Fabric endorsement-policy satisfaction

questions.question: What is the ordering service's main role in a typical Fabric transaction flow?

options.text: Order transactions, package them into blocks, and distribute them
Directly execute all chaincode to produce endorsement responses
Receive private-collection plaintext and distribute it to all channel peers
Check each peer's read set and directly finalize the writes

questions.explanation: Chaincode simulation and endorsement, transaction ordering, and commit validation are distinct stages. The ordering service handles ordering and block delivery.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding the Fabric ordering service

questions.question: A key read by Fabric transaction T is updated by another valid transaction before T is validated. What happens if T's read version no longer matches?

options.text: The ordering service automatically edits T's inputs and re-signs it
T may be marked invalid during validation, and its write set is not applied
The version difference is always ignored because the key exists
T's endorsement signatures always let it overwrite using the old value

questions.explanation: Fabric checks read-set version consistency during validation. If state changes after simulation, even an endorsed transaction may not be applied.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding Fabric read-version conflicts

questions.question: What is the typical sharing scope when using a Fabric private data collection?

options.text: Plaintext goes to authorized peers, while verification hashes go to the channel ledger
Plaintext is permanently stored only by the ordering service and cannot be seen by peers
Plaintext hashes disappear, and each organization independently changes values
Plaintext and hashes are always public to all internet users

questions.explanation: Private data is distributed to organizations according to the collection policy. Hashes on the channel ledger help verify the data's existence and integrity.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding Fabric private data and hashes

questions.question: Which statement distinguishes the world state from the blockchain transaction history in a Fabric ledger?

options.text: They are aliases for the same file and have no difference in role
Block history keeps only the latest values and overwrites all past transactions
World state stores every historical version as a single value for each key
World state holds the latest key values, while block history holds ordered records of changes

questions.explanation: World state enables efficient queries of current state, while block history preserves the transactions that produced that state.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing world state from block history

questions.question: A hypothetical token trades at KRW 250 and has a circulating supply of 2 million. What is its circulating market capitalization?
questions.explanation: KRW 250 × 2,000,000 tokens = KRW 500,000,000, or KRW 500 million. First make sure the supply and price units match.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding token valuation calculations and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Using the same current price, calculations use a circulating supply of 2 million and a maximum supply of 10 million. How many times circulating market capitalization is FDV?
questions.explanation: With the same price, the ratio between the valuations equals the supply ratio. 10 million ÷ 2 million = 5. This does not predict that the future price will remain unchanged.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding token valuation calculations and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Assume circulating market capitalization stays constant. If only circulating supply doubles, what happens to the token price?
questions.explanation: Market capitalization = price × circulating supply, so price is inversely proportional to circulating supply when valuation is fixed. This follows the question's assumption and is not a real-world price forecast.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding token valuation calculations and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A total of 60,000 tokens is released in equal monthly amounts over 24 months from the starting date. With no cliff or upfront release, how many have cumulatively vested at the end of month 3?
questions.explanation: Each month releases 60,000 ÷ 24 = 2,500 tokens, giving 7,500 over 3 months. The amount actually claimable additionally subtracts tokens already received.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding vesting calculations and their applicable conditions

questions.question: An allocation of 40,000 tokens specifies a one-time release of 25% when a 12-month cliff ends. With no earlier release, how many are released at that exact moment?
questions.explanation: Applying the stated cliff-release percentage gives 40,000 × 0.25 = 10,000 tokens. It is important to distinguish linear vesting from a release of a specified percentage.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding vesting calculations and their applicable conditions

questions.question: You hold 1,000 of a total 100,000 tokens. Another 25,000 are newly issued to other people while your quantity stays unchanged. What is your share of the total supply?
questions.explanation: Total supply after issuance is 125,000. Your share is 1,000 ÷ 125,000 × 100 = 0.8%. The share is diluted even though your quantity is unchanged.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding ownership dilution and its applicable conditions

questions.question: Initial total supply is 1 million tokens. Then 80,000 are issued and 30,000 are actually burned. With no other changes, what is final total supply?
questions.explanation: 1,000,000 + 80,000 − 30,000 = 1,050,000 tokens. Even with a burn, net supply rises if issuance is greater.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding supply calculations and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Assume all 1 million unlocked tokens newly enter circulation alongside the current circulating supply of 4 million. What is the percentage increase in circulating supply?
questions.explanation: The denominator for growth is the original circulating supply. 1 million ÷ 4 million = 25%, distinct from the unlocked tokens' 20% share of the final supply.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding circulating-supply calculations and their applicable conditions

questions.question: You buy 2 tokens at KRW 100 each and 3 at KRW 120 each. Excluding fees, what is the average purchase price?
questions.explanation: Total spending is 2×100 + 3×120 = KRW 560 for 5 tokens. 560 ÷ 5 = KRW 112. The simple average of the two prices is not appropriate.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding average purchase prices and their applicable conditions

questions.question: You sell 5 tokens for KRW 700 after buying them for a total of KRW 560. Assume both the purchase and sale incur a 1% transaction fee and there are no taxes. What is the net profit?
questions.explanation: The purchase cost is KRW 565.6, and sale proceeds are KRW 693. Net profit is 693 − 565.6 = KRW 127.4, including costs on both sides.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding net profit and loss calculations and their applicable conditions

questions.question: The asks are 1 token at KRW 100 and 2 tokens at KRW 101. With no other changes, what is the average execution price excluding fees for a market buy of 3 tokens?
questions.explanation: The total execution value is 100×1 + 101×2 = KRW 302. Dividing by 3 gives approximately KRW 100.67, a quantity-weighted average.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding order-book execution and its applicable conditions

questions.question: The best bid is KRW 99 and the best ask is KRW 101. What is the spread as a percentage of the midpoint?
questions.explanation: The midpoint is (99+101)/2 = KRW 100, and the spread is KRW 2. Thus, 2 ÷ 100 × 100 = 2%.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding spread calculations and their applicable conditions

questions.question: You want to trade only the quantity that can execute immediately and cancel the rest. Which order condition fits?
questions.explanation: IOC executes the immediately available portion and cancels the remaining quantity. It differs from FOK, which requires an immediate full fill or complete cancellation.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding order execution conditions and when they apply

questions.question: You do not want any units traded unless your order for 10 units can fill completely and immediately. Which condition fits?
questions.explanation: FOK requires the entire quantity to execute immediately under the specified conditions. Its requirement differs from IOC, which allows a partial fill.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding order execution conditions and when they apply

questions.question: A post-only limit buy would immediately match an existing ask when submitted. If the exchange's rule rejects orders that would execute immediately, what happens?

options.text: It reverses into a market sell
It executes immediately with the maker fee

questions.explanation: The post-only rule in this question restricts the order to providing resting liquidity. If its price would immediately make it a taker, it is rejected without execution.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding order execution conditions and when they apply

questions.question: A stop-limit sell has a stop price of KRW 100 and a limit price of KRW 98. The price drops sharply from KRW 105 to KRW 90, with no bids at KRW 98 or higher. What can happen?

options.text: It necessarily fills in full at KRW 100
The order can trigger but remain unfilled
It necessarily fills in full at KRW 98

questions.explanation: Meeting the stop condition creates the limit order. Actual execution still requires buyers willing to take the quantity at or above the limit price.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding order risks and their applicable conditions

questions.question: ETH/BTC is quoted at 0.05 BTC, and you buy 2 ETH. Excluding fees, how much BTC do you pay?
questions.explanation: The price expresses BTC per 1 ETH. 0.05 × 2 = 0.1 BTC. Distinguish the traded asset's units from the quote currency.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding trading-pair calculations and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A buy order initially requests 10 tokens. After 4 fill, cancellation of the remainder succeeds. How many tokens have you acquired?
questions.explanation: Successful cancellation applies to the quantity still unfilled. You retain the 4 tokens that already filled.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding execution history and its applicable conditions

questions.question: In a linear contract, you open a long position of 3 units at USD 100 each and close it at USD 110. Excluding costs, what is the profit or loss?
questions.explanation: A linear long's profit or loss is quantity × (exit price − entry price). 3 × (110−100) = USD 30. Do not confuse the position's total value with its profit.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding derivatives profit and loss and the applicable conditions

questions.question: In a linear contract, you open a short position of 2 units at USD 100 each and close it at USD 90. Excluding costs, what is the profit or loss?
questions.explanation: For a linear short, multiply quantity by entry price minus exit price. 2 × (100−90) = USD 20, so a price decline produces a profit.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding derivatives profit and loss and the applicable conditions

questions.question: You maintain a USD 500 linear long position with USD 100 of equity. If the price falls 4%, ignoring costs and liquidation, what percentage of equity is lost?
questions.explanation: The position loses 500 × 0.04 = USD 20. That is 20% of the USD 100 equity. Five-times leverage increases sensitivity to losses.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding leverage calculations and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A long position with a notional value of USD 20,000 must pay 0.01% for one funding interval. How much funding does it pay?
questions.explanation: 0.01% is 0.0001 as a decimal. 20,000 × 0.0001 = USD 2. The question explicitly specifies that the long pays.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding funding calculations and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Spot is USD 100 and futures are USD 103 at the same moment. What is the basis percentage using spot price as the denominator?
questions.explanation: Under the specified definition, (103−100) ÷ 100 = 3%. Using the futures price as the denominator produces a different result, so check the definition first.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding basis calculations and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A portfolio worth KRW 1 million falls 20% to KRW 800,000. What percentage increase from its current value is needed to recover the original amount?
questions.explanation: Recovery requires KRW 200,000 from a current base of KRW 800,000. 200,000 ÷ 800,000 = 25%, so a loss percentage and its required recovery percentage generally differ.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding loss recovery and its applicable conditions

questions.question: You deposit 1,000 tokens at 12% annual simple interest for exactly half a year. If the rate is fixed and there are no costs, how many reward tokens are earned?
questions.explanation: Rewards equal principal × annual rate × time: 1,000 × 0.12 × 0.5 = 60 tokens. The figure 1,060 includes the principal.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding simple-interest rewards and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Rewards of 2% are paid each quarter and immediately reinvested in full. If the rate stays fixed for a year, what is the annual return in token quantity?
questions.explanation: The annual growth factor is 1.02 to the fourth power. 1.02^4−1 = 0.08243216, approximately 8.24%, rather than the simple sum of 8%.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding compound rewards and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A deposit earns 50 tokens in gross rewards, and the operator takes 10% of the rewards as a fee. With no fee on principal, what is the net reward?
questions.explanation: The reward fee is 50×10% = 5 tokens. The user receives 50−5 = 45 in net rewards. The condition does not deduct 10% of principal.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding reward fees and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Token quantity increases by 10%, while its KRW price falls 20%. With no other changes, how does the KRW valuation change?
questions.explanation: The valuation factor is 1.10×0.80 = 0.88, a 12% decrease from the initial value. Token-quantity rewards alone do not determine KRW returns.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding valuation returns and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Assume with certainty that one reinvestment increases future rewards by USD 3 and immediately costs USD 5 in gas. What is its net effect?
questions.explanation: Subtracting the added cost from the added income gives 3−5 = −USD 2. Even with compounding, the net effect is unfavorable when reinvestment costs more than the benefit.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding reinvestment costs and their applicable conditions

questions.question: You hold 100 tokens targeting USD 1, and they continue to trade at exactly USD 1. If only the exchange rate moves from KRW 1,300 to KRW 1,400 per dollar, how does their valuation change?
questions.explanation: The initial value is 100×1,300 = KRW 130,000, and the later value is KRW 140,000. Stable USD pricing and stable KRW valuation are different concepts.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding exchange-rate valuation and its applicable conditions

questions.question: After a proportional rebase, your balance rises from 100 to 110 tokens and total supply rises from 1,000 to 1,100. What happens to your share of supply?
questions.explanation: Before and after the rebase, 100/1,000 and 110/1,100 both equal 10%. An increased quantity does not always mean an increased relative share.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding rebasing and its applicable conditions

questions.question: You hold 10 non-rebasing deposit receipt tokens. If the redeemable assets per receipt token increase from 1 to 1.05, what is the total redemption amount?
questions.explanation: The receipt-token quantity stays unchanged while the exchange rate increases. 10×1.05 = 10.5 assets. Rewards can be reflected in a redemption ratio instead of a higher token quantity.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding exchange-rate receipt tokens and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A token has a protocol redemption reference of 1 ETH but trades for 0.97 ETH in the market. What is the discount relative to that reference?
questions.explanation: The price is 0.03 ETH below the 1 ETH reference, so 0.03/1 = 3%. Check actual redemption timing and costs alongside the market discount.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding LST discounts and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Contractual liabilities are USD 1 million, and liquidating reserve assets yields USD 980,000. With no other funding, what is the shortfall?
questions.explanation: 1,000,000 − 980,000 = USD 20,000. This illustrates that reserve assets' book face value can differ from their realizable liquidation value.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding backing reserves and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A token structure lets its issuer block transfers by particular addresses. Which risk should users examine?

options.text: The risk of private keys becoming shorter
The risk of block height automatically decreasing
Transfer restrictions imposed through freeze authority
The risk of every exchange price becoming fixed at zero

questions.explanation: Issuer controls can affect token usability. Being transferred on a public blockchain does not give every token the same censorship resistance.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding permission risks and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Already-staked assets are also used to secure another validation service. What needs additional review compared with basic staking?

options.text: The additional service's slashing conditions and shared loss paths
Only whether the token logo changes

questions.explanation: Restaking can add separate validation duties and penalties in pursuit of more rewards. New conditions may overlap with the risks of basic staking.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding restaking and its applicable conditions

questions.question: Validator operators A and B share the same cloud region and failure causes. What limits the benefit of splitting a stake between them?

options.text: Shared failure risk remains even though there are two names
A shared failure doubles the token quantity
Two companies necessarily have independent failures
The server count is always zero regardless of consensus

questions.explanation: The number of operators differs from the independence of failure causes. Overlapping infrastructure, clients, or administrative keys can cause simultaneous problems.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding staking diversification and its applicable conditions

questions.question: An exchange proves it holds KRW 12 billion in assets but does not disclose its total customer liabilities. What is the most justified conclusion?

options.text: That evidence alone cannot show whether assets cover all liabilities
Customer liabilities are exactly KRW 10 billion

questions.explanation: Assessing solvency requires comparing assets with total liabilities. Disclosing only one side does not reveal the ratio or omitted obligations.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding proof of reserves and its applicable conditions

questions.question: Of 1,000 total voting units, 200 participate, with 150 in favor and 50 against. If the participation quorum is 300, what is the result?

options.text: The proposal necessarily executes immediately because 75% favor it
150 votes in favor equal a quorum of 300
The quorum is not met even though more votes are in favor

questions.explanation: Actual participation is 200, below the required 300. Distinguish the 75% approval share among votes cast from the 20% participation rate relative to total voting power.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding voting participation and its applicable conditions

questions.question: A system lets a user delegate voting weight to a representative without transferring tokens. What does the representative receive?

options.text: The ability to exercise voting power under the rules
The delegator's private keys for withdrawing every token

questions.explanation: Delegating votes differs from approving token transfers. Whether withdrawal authority also changes must be checked through separate interfaces and permissions.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding voting-power delegation and its applicable conditions

questions.question: A simple pool deducts a 0.3% swap fee from input and uses the remainder for price calculation. Of an input of 1,000 tokens, what is the effective input?
questions.explanation: The fee is 1,000×0.003 = 3 tokens, leaving an effective input of 997. Take care when converting a percentage to a decimal.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding AMM fees and their applicable conditions

questions.question: In a constant-product pool with no fees or other trades, why is the average execution price of one large buy worse than the pre-trade spot price?

options.text: The token loses decimal places during the trade
A central bank fixes every pool's price
Transaction signatures are always required twice
The reserve ratio keeps changing during the trade

questions.explanation: Assets are received along the constant-product curve, so later units become more expensive as trade size increases. A trade creates its own price impact even without external price changes.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding AMM price impact and its applicable conditions

questions.question: For an exact-input swap, a user sets a minimum output of 95 tokens. If the final calculated output is 94, what should the protective logic do?

options.text: Give 94 and always mark the swap successful
Change the private key and execute again
Mint the difference to bring output to 95

questions.explanation: The minimum output is the user's acceptable lower bound. Rejecting a trade that cannot meet it protects the user from unfavorable execution.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding swap conditions and when they apply

questions.question: For an exact-output swap, the maximum input is set to 100 tokens to receive 10 tokens. What should happen if the required input rises to 103?

options.text: Use the next block's private key
Set output to zero and mark the swap successful
Fail because the permitted input is exceeded

questions.explanation: In an exact-output trade, the spending cap protects the user. If the required input exceeds that cap, execution should fail instead of spending without authorization.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding swap conditions and when they apply

questions.question: A DEX order's deadline has long passed, although its minimum-output condition is satisfied. With expiry checks implemented correctly, what happens?

options.text: The deadline is automatically extended by a year
It is rejected because the deadline has passed
The approved private key is deleted
It always executes because the price condition is met

questions.explanation: The deadline and price limit are independent conditions. The deadline must also be checked to prevent stale orders from executing later.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding swap deadlines and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A proportional pool has 900 existing shares. A new investor deposits assets in the same ratio and receives 100 new shares. What is the investor's final ownership share?
questions.explanation: Total shares after the deposit are 900+100 = 1,000. The new investor's share is 100/1,000 = 10%; existing shares alone are not the denominator.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding LP shares and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Two Uniswap v3-style positions have different price ranges. What matters when allocating trading fees?

options.text: Their relative amounts of liquidity active at the traded price
Only the original token quantities deposited by all positions
The length of each position creator's name
The rarity of the NFT image

questions.explanation: Liquidity within the range where a trade occurs participates in pricing and fee allocation. Equal total deposits can produce different outcomes depending on active ranges.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding concentrated liquidity and its applicable conditions

questions.question: Only token A depegs in a pool containing dollar-linked tokens A and B. What risk should an LP understand?

options.text: Arbitrage may leave the LP holding more of the weakened token A
Loss is impossible because both assets target the dollar
Every LP share automatically becomes dollar cash
B's private key changes into A

questions.explanation: When relative external prices change, traders change the pool's asset composition. Pools of linked assets remain exposed to deterioration in one asset's value.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding correlated-asset pools and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A user deposits an asset into protocol A and then uses its receipt token as collateral in protocol B. What should be considered when simply adding A's and B's TVL?

options.text: The same underlying economic value may be counted twice
The original deposit is automatically canceled
Price information is no longer needed
The underlying asset is necessarily issued twice

questions.explanation: Connected protocols' TVL may count both the same underlying asset and its receipt token. The sum is not necessarily equal to new net capital arriving from outside.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding TVL double counting and its applicable conditions

questions.question: A pool earns little in trading fees, and most of its advertised yield comes from newly issued reward tokens. What is the key analysis?

options.text: Yield sustainability when emissions fall and the reward token's price
Whether the token name is capitalized

questions.explanation: New-token subsidies differ from income generated by actual use of a service. Changes in emissions or token prices can substantially alter displayed yields.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding sources of DeFi yield and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A hypothetical lending service has collateral worth USD 2,000 and a 60% LTV cap for new borrowing. With no other debt, what is the maximum new loan?
questions.explanation: The new borrowing limit is collateral value×LTV: 2,000×0.60=USD 1,200. The liquidation threshold and the limit for new borrowing can be different settings.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding borrowing limits and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Of 1,000 tokens supplied to a lending pool, 800 are lent out. If utilization is defined as borrowed amount/total supply, what is utilization?
questions.explanation: Utilization is 800÷1,000×100=80%. This does not mean all pool assets can be withdrawn immediately; actual idle liquidity must be checked separately.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding lending utilization and its applicable conditions

questions.question: Use the simplified formula supply rate=borrow rate×utilization×(1−reserve factor). With a 10% borrow rate, 80% utilization, and a 10% reserve factor, what is the supply rate?
questions.explanation: 0.10×0.80×0.90=0.072, or 7.2% annually. Actual protocol rate formulas and reward-token payments may differ from this simplified model.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding lending interest rates and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Under a hypothetical rule, repaying USD 100 of debt earns collateral worth the repaid amount plus 5%. What is the collateral value received by the liquidator?
questions.explanation: The liquidator receives collateral worth 100×1.05=USD 105. Actual net profit requires subtracting transaction fees and collateral-selling costs.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding liquidation bonuses and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A hypothetical service allows at most 40% of current debt to be liquidated in one action. For debt of USD 500, what is the maximum repayment in one action?
questions.explanation: 500×0.40=USD 200. Partial-liquidation limits vary by service and account state, so apply only the 40% specified here.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding partial liquidation and its applicable conditions

questions.question: A hypothetical flash loan lends 100,000 tokens at a fee of 0.05%. What total must be returned within the same transaction?
questions.explanation: The fee is 100,000×0.0005=50 tokens, making the total repayment 100,050. Actual fees are protocol settings; this calculation uses the stated rate.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding flash-loan fees and their applicable conditions

questions.question: An isolation mode limits the assets that can be borrowed and total debt against a particular collateral asset. What is the main purpose?

options.text: Permanently remove price volatility from isolated collateral
Limit how far the collateral's risk can spread across the lending market
Transfer every borrower's private keys to the operator

questions.explanation: Isolation mode restricts borrowing exposure created by risky collateral. It does not make the collateral safe or eliminate potential losses.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding risk isolation and its applicable conditions

questions.question: A token has a supply cap of 1,000, with 950 currently deposited. Partial deposits are allowed and nothing else changes. What is the largest additional deposit?
questions.explanation: The remaining capacity is 1,000−950=50 tokens. A supply cap controls market size; owning tokens in a wallet does not mean all of them can be deposited.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding supply caps and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A user sends 100 tokens to a contract, but a transfer tax increases the contract's balance by only 98. Which value should be credited to reflect the amount actually received?

options.text: The contract's before-and-after balance increase of 98

questions.explanation: Fee-on-transfer tokens can deliver a different amount from the requested quantity. Check received amounts through balance changes while also considering other behaviors such as rebasing.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding fee-on-transfer tokens and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Some tokens return no value from transfer and are incompatible with ordinary bool-checking code. Which library should be considered for integration?
questions.explanation: SafeERC20 improves call compatibility with various ERC-20 implementations, including tokens with no return value. It does not itself guarantee economic safety or cover every nonstandard behavior.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding ERC-20 compatibility and its applicable conditions

questions.question: Token A has 6 decimals and token B has 18. Both raw balances are 1,000,000. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: B always has a larger display quantity because it has more decimals
A is 1,000,000 tokens and B is 18 tokens
Both are 1 token, so their display quantities are equal
A is 1 token and B is 0.000000000001 tokens; raw integers alone cannot be compared as quantities

questions.explanation: Display quantities divide raw balances by each token's 10^decimals. A is 10^6/10^6=1 and B is 10^6/10^18=10^-12. Comparing values also requires separate prices for the assets.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding token-unit comparisons and their applicable conditions

questions.question: An ERC-2981 implementation returns a royalty of 2.5% of the sale price. For a sale price of 2 ETH, what is the specified royalty?
questions.explanation: 2×0.025=0.05 ETH. ERC-2981 communicates royalty information; it does not force actual payment through every sales route.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding NFT royalty calculations and their applicable conditions

questions.question: For an ERC-4907 NFT, owner A assigns user B an expiry of tomorrow. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Assigning B necessarily burns A's ownership immediately
Every NFT standard already mandates the same rental feature
B owns the NFT regardless of expiry
Use rights can be separated from ownership to grant B time-limited use

questions.explanation: ERC-4907 adds user and expires information to separate the user role from the owner. Check how the actual service interprets and enforces those rights.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding NFT rentals and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Tokens are only sent to an address whose key nobody knows, while the contract's totalSupply remains unchanged. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Changing the receiving address also decreases decimals
totalSupply necessarily falls by the transferred amount
A transfer alone does not automatically guarantee a reduction in totalSupply
Every balance increases in the same proportion

questions.explanation: An ordinary transfer changes which address holds a balance and differs from a burn function that reduces totalSupply. Tokens locked at an inaccessible address may be treated separately depending on the definition of supply statistics.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding burn accounting and its applicable conditions

questions.question: You are developing a lending contract that receives tokens which call recipient contracts. Beyond simple balance accounting, what should be checked carefully?

options.text: External calls and possible reentrancy during transfers
The number of consonants in the token name
The width of the token logo file

questions.explanation: If a token transfer executes external code, it may call back into the contract during state updates. Review supported token behaviors alongside the order of state changes.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding token hooks and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A parent transaction is 200 vB with a 200 sat fee, and its child is 100 vB with a 700 sat fee. What is their combined fee rate?
questions.explanation: Total fees of 900 sat divided by total size of 300 vB give 3 sat/vB. This alone does not guarantee relay or mining; node package policies also matter.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding CPFP fees and their applicable conditions

questions.question: An exchange combines several customers' Bitcoin withdrawals into multiple outputs of one transaction. Which statement correctly pairs an expected benefit with a concern?

options.text: It can reduce some shared costs but reveal links between withdrawals
Every output must have the same recipient
Multiple outputs make a transaction invalid under consensus
Fees always become zero and all recipients become anonymous

questions.explanation: Batching can save costs by sharing transaction overhead. Combining withdrawals into one transaction can also make relationships between addresses easier to observe.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding batched withdrawals and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A recovery phrase is correct, but a particular Bitcoin account's balance does not appear. What additional settings should be checked?

options.text: The derivation path, address type, account number, and additional passphrase
Only whether the token logo was downloaded

questions.explanation: The same seed can generate different address sets when the derivation path, address type, or account number differs. If a BIP-39 passphrase was used, it must also match.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding wallet recovery paths and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A hardware wallet requests a PSBT signature. What should be checked most directly before signing?

options.text: Recipient address, payment amount, fee, and change outputs
Whether the internet connection icon is green
Whether the wallet case recently changed color
Whether the filename includes the word success

questions.explanation: PSBT is a format containing transaction information to sign, not a certificate guaranteeing that the content is safe. Check the transaction destination, costs, and other details shown on the device.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding PSBT review and its applicable conditions

questions.question: One Bitcoin node declines to relay a transaction. What conclusion cannot be drawn from that fact alone?

options.text: The node's policy may need to be checked
Its fee policy may have played a role
The transaction is necessarily invalid under consensus rules
That node did not relay that transaction

questions.explanation: Relay policies may impose restrictions beyond consensus validity. Policy rejection and consensus invalidity should not be treated as equivalent.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding node policies and their applicable conditions

questions.question: What does an account's owner field generally represent in Solana?

options.text: The administrator of the entire network
A personal wallet always identical to the account address
The program that governs the account's data

questions.explanation: In Solana, owner means the program that owns the account, not a person's legal ownership. It also differs from the token-holder field stored within a token account.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding Solana account owners and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Why are token accounts for receiving USDC and another token distinct even when the same user's SOL address is unchanged?

options.text: The SOL address is deleted every second
A token account is associated with a particular mint and holder
Every token has the same mint

questions.explanation: A token account records who holds tokens of a particular mint. Assets from different mints are managed in distinct token accounts even for the same wallet holder.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding Solana token accounts and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A Solana program manages an asset vault using a PDA. Which statement correctly describes PDA signing authority?

options.text: Anyone knowing the PDA address can sign
A PDA can sign for every program
The operator downloads the PDA's private key into an ordinary wallet
The program obtains signer authority through the runtime using the correct seeds

questions.explanation: A PDA differs from an ordinary account address with a private key. The program used in its derivation exercises PDA signer authority through the correct seeds and runtime calls.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding PDA usage and its applicable conditions

questions.question: The last of three instructions in one Solana transaction fails. How are account-state changes generally handled?

options.text: Failure changes every related private key
Only the last instruction automatically re-executes in another block
The first two instructions always remain committed and no fees apply
The transaction's state changes are rolled back, but fees may still apply

questions.explanation: Instructions within a transaction execute atomically, so an instruction failure cancels the transaction's state changes. Charging fees for a failed transaction is a separate matter.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding Solana atomicity and its applicable conditions

questions.question: A signed Solana transaction is submitted after its recent blockhash has expired. What is a reasonable response?

options.text: An expired transaction always becomes valid if its fee is raised without limit
Replace only the blockhash without changing the expired signature bytes
Check the current state, rebuild the transaction with a new blockhash, and sign again

questions.explanation: Recent blockhashes are used for transaction validity periods and replay prevention. If the signed message changes, the old signature cannot be reused, so rebuilding and re-signing are necessary.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding blockhash expiry and its applicable conditions

questions.question: Assume priority fee=ceil(CU limit×CU price/1,000,000) lamports. With 200,000 CU and 1,000 micro-lamports/CU, what is the priority fee?
questions.explanation: 200,000×1,000÷1,000,000=200 lamports. This is the priority fee calculated in the question; a base fee may be added separately.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding compute-unit pricing and its applicable conditions

questions.question: A Solana token's freeze authority remains enabled. What risk should be reviewed?

options.text: The risk that anyone can delete every SOL account
The risk that the mint address necessarily changes every day
The risk that token decimal places automatically increase without limit
Whether the authority can freeze token accounts and the policy governing that power

questions.explanation: Freeze authority can restrict transfers and other actions for particular token accounts. It is separate from mint authority; check the actual settings and authority holder.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding freeze authority and its applicable conditions

questions.question: What does a relayer generally do in IBC communication?

options.text: Fix the market price of tokens
Arbitrarily finalize the other chain's consensus without verifying proofs
Hold every private key on both chains
Deliver proofs, headers, packets, and related data from the other chain

questions.explanation: Relayers transport messages and proofs between chains. Delivering a message differs from the receiving chain verifying its proof.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding IBC relayers and their applicable conditions

questions.question: An IBC transfer packet meets timeout conditions. What is required for safe follow-up handling?

options.text: Any relayer pressing a refund button without a signature
Only confirmation that a price chart has fallen
Verifiable timeout proofs and state checks required by the protocol
Only the sender's verbal cancellation request

questions.explanation: Timeout processing resolves a transfer using the states of both chains and proofs. Failing to check whether delivery occurred and whether timeout processing is valid can cause duplicate handling.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding IBC timeouts and their applicable conditions

questions.question: USDC with the same display name has arrived through different bridge routes. What should be checked before treating it as the same asset?

options.text: Only its display order in a wallet
Only the token icon's file size
The chain, token contract, issuer, and backing or redemption route
Only the number of capital letters in its name

questions.explanation: A matching name or symbol does not establish the same issuance or backing relationship. Check whether the asset is natively issued or a bridged representation, along with its redemption structure.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding bridge routes and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A price feed returns answer=250,000,000,000 and decimals=8. What is the display price?
questions.explanation: Dividing 250,000,000,000 by 10^8 gives 2,500. Confusing raw price integers with display units can cause major errors in collateral valuation and other calculations.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding oracle decimals and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A hypothetical contract uses a feed only for 60 minutes after its last update. The latest update was 75 minutes ago. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Update the price by changing decimals to 0
Turn the past price into a current price by raising fees
Restrict the transaction or use an alternative route under the defined stale-price policy
Always use it solely because the price is positive

questions.explanation: Validate the update time, such as updatedAt, as well as the price value. A service must define its stop or fallback policy for stale values in advance.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding oracle freshness and its applicable conditions

questions.question: Over a 10-minute period, the price is 100 for 6 minutes and 120 for 4 minutes. What is the simple time-weighted average price?
questions.explanation: The time-weighted average is (100×6+120×4)÷10=108. Actual oracles may use arithmetic or geometric averages and other methods, so follow the question's definition.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding time-weighted averages and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A lending service detects an abnormal price move over a short period and pauses only new borrowing. What is the main purpose?

options.text: Limit further risk exposure caused by the abnormal price
Mathematically erase every loss that has already occurred
Fix the collateral price across the entire market
Automatically recover from a private-key leak

questions.explanation: Pausing new borrowing reduces risk expansion during bad valuations or rapid changes. Whether all functions should stop, and whether repayments or collateral additions remain allowed, are separate policy decisions.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding circuit breakers and their applicable conditions

questions.question: You want to avoid crediting an event from the same block twice when an Ethereum log is redelivered. Which identification key is appropriate?

options.text: The combination of chain ID, block hash, transaction hash, and log index
Only the block's timestamp rounded to a minute

questions.explanation: A transaction can contain several logs, so its hash alone may be insufficient. Include the block hash to distinguish inclusion locations and separately handle reversals caused by reorganizations.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding indexer deduplication and its applicable conditions

questions.question: The block containing a deposit credited by an indexer is removed from the canonical chain. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Reverse that block's credited effects and reapply the canonical chain state
Permanently confirm the deposit because it appeared on-screen once
Credit the same log once more
Restore the historical block by changing the recipient address's private key

questions.explanation: Handling reorganizations requires per-block change histories and rollback procedures. Confirmation policies can reduce risk but cannot replace an indexer's reorganization handling.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding reorganization handling and its applicable conditions

questions.question: A network error leads a user to retry the same withdrawal request. Which server design prevents duplicate withdrawals?

options.text: Store a request idempotency key and reuse the existing processing result
Always make the response time zero seconds
Always create a new withdrawal for each retry

questions.explanation: An idempotency key helps treat retries of the same business request as one operation. Preventing duplicate blockchain transaction hashes differs from preventing a server from creating two different transactions.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding withdrawal-request idempotency and its applicable conditions

questions.question: An Ethereum receipt has a successful status, but the user did not receive the expected swap amount. What is the most appropriate check?

options.text: Assume successful transactions necessarily pay 0 ETH in fees
Skip checking because status guarantees every expected return
Inspect executed functions, events, and balance changes against the intended business outcome
Have the user directly change status to failure

questions.explanation: Success means execution did not revert, not that every economic expectation was met. Specify conditions such as a minimum output in the transaction and inspect the actual result.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding transaction receipts and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Two contracts on different chains have the same 0x address. Which conclusion is appropriate?

options.text: Validation on one chain guarantees every permission on the other
Matching addresses necessarily have identical stored state
The code and state deployed on each chain must be checked to determine whether they represent the same service
Matching addresses automatically move assets between the chains

questions.explanation: Identical addresses on different chains can have different code and state. Check the chain ID, deployment information, and administrative powers alongside the address.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding contract-address comparisons and their applicable conditions

questions.question: The lowest NFT ask is 1 ETH, but the only bid is 0.6 ETH. Which statement about an immediately achievable sale price is correct?

options.text: Every holder can immediately sell at 1 ETH
A floor price of 1 ETH does not guarantee an immediately achievable sale price
An ask means no buyer is needed

questions.explanation: The floor price usually means the lowest listed asking price. Actual sales depend on buyer demand, individual NFT characteristics, and market conditions.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding NFT floor prices and their applicable conditions

questions.question: What can a marketplace do after receiving an ERC-4906 MetadataUpdate event?

options.text: Transfer ownership arbitrarily based only on the event
Query the NFT's metadata again and refresh its display

questions.explanation: ERC-4906 defines an event interface for announcing metadata changes. Such notifications are different from ownership transfers or royalty payments.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding NFT metadata and its applicable conditions

questions.question: A hypothetical rule sets quorum at 20% of 1,000 voting units and counts votes for plus against as participation. With 120 for and 60 against, is quorum met?

options.text: The 120 votes for exceed total voting power
It is necessarily met because votes for exceed votes against
Votes against make quorum impossible to calculate
No: 180 total votes fall short of 200

questions.explanation: Quorum is 1,000×20%=200 votes, while participation is 120+60=180. Majority support and minimum participation are separate requirements.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding voting quorums and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A hypothetical DAO requires a 48-hour delay from scheduling execution. What is the earliest execution time for an operation scheduled at 10:00 on Monday?
questions.explanation: 48 hours is two days, so the time is 10:00 on Wednesday in the same time zone. This calculation assumes no other conditions such as a voting period before scheduling.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding timelock waiting periods and their applicable conditions

questions.question: One key in a 3-of-5 multisignature vault is compromised, while the others remain independently secure. Which immediate assessment is appropriate?

options.text: One leaked key always generates all five signatures
The one compromised key cannot meet the threshold, but a response such as key rotation is needed
The other four keys are necessarily compromised mathematically
3-of-5 means anyone can withdraw by clicking three times

questions.explanation: Three valid signatures are required, so one key alone cannot authorize withdrawal. Nevertheless, the remaining safety margin is reduced, making key rotation and log review necessary.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding multisignature authorization and its applicable conditions

questions.question: An exchange's internal screen shows a balance, but on-chain withdrawals are paused. What cannot be established from that balance alone?

options.text: That the custody structure needs to be distinguished
That the user can directly move those assets now using a private key
That the withdrawal status needs additional checking
That the exchange displays a balance in the account

questions.explanation: A custodial account's ledger balance differs from an on-chain balance immediately controlled by the user's private key. More information is needed about the withdrawal pause and the asset-liability structure.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding custodial-asset distinctions and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Of a USD 1,000 portfolio, USD 600 is in asset A. If only A falls 25% and all other assets stay unchanged, what is the total portfolio value?
questions.explanation: A loses 600×25%=USD 150, leaving total assets of USD 850. Even with multiple assets, losses vary with correlation and concentration.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding diversification calculations and their applicable conditions

questions.question: Buying on exchange A and selling on B is expected to earn a USD 20 price spread, but total fees are USD 8 and expected slippage is USD 15. What is the expected net result?
questions.explanation: Expected net profit or loss is 20−8−15=−USD 3. Additional risks such as transfer delays and price changes further mean that the displayed spread alone cannot guarantee profit.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding arbitrage costs and their applicable conditions

questions.question: A linear position has a value of USD 1,000 and net equity of USD 200. With the position and price unchanged, another USD 100 of collateral is added. What is the leverage?
questions.explanation: Defining leverage as position notional/net equity gives 1,000÷300≈3.33 times. Adding collateral reduces leverage for the same position rather than eliminating price risk.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding leverage reduction and its applicable conditions

questions.question: An exchange presents a signature proving control of a wallet address at a particular time. What does this alone not prove?

options.text: Solvency including all customer liabilities and whether assets are encumbered
That there is a valid signature for the specified message
That a public address has been provided for verification
That the proof is linked to a particular message

questions.explanation: Proof of address control does not fully account for omitted liabilities, borrowed reserves, or other creditors' claims. Solvency assessment requires assets, total liabilities, and associated rights to be considered together.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding proof scope and its applicable conditions

questions.question: A project's white paper says there are no administrative powers, but its deployed contract has an administrator function for minting additional tokens. What should take priority?

options.text: Do not inspect deployed code if the white paper contains the claim
The white paper automatically changes how every deployed contract operates
An administrator function cannot execute if the token symbol is short
Check the deployed code and permission settings, and record the inconsistency with the white paper

questions.explanation: Documentation may not match executable code. Check the contract address, code version, current role holders, and upgrade paths.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding white-paper verification and its applicable conditions

questions.question: A failed low-level Solidity call can return false as its success flag, so the caller must explicitly check the return value.
questions.explanation: A low-level call does not always automatically propagate failure as an exception in the enclosing call. Ignoring its result can let the app continue in an unintended state.
questions.learningObjective: Handling return values from failed low-level calls

questions.question: Reusing the same Bitcoin receiving address can make it easier to infer that multiple payments are associated with the same recipient.
questions.explanation: Repeated use of an address in public transaction records provides clues linking transactions. Using new addresses alone does not guarantee complete anonymity.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding address reuse and transaction linkability

questions.question: Every correctly operating Bitcoin node must always hold exactly the same set of unconfirmed transactions.
questions.explanation: Unconfirmed transaction sets can differ with propagation timing, connectivity, and local policy. Block consensus state differs from a node's local waiting list.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing the mempool from consensus state

questions.question: In BIP-39, using the same normalized recovery phrase and the same passphrase reproduces the same generated seed.
questions.explanation: BIP-39 uses specified normalization and key-derivation procedures. Identical inputs produce the same seed, while subsequent addresses also depend on derivation rules.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding reproducible seed generation

questions.question: Even if an ERC-2612 signature passes cryptographic verification, a permit call after its deadline must be rejected.
questions.explanation: In addition to matching the signer, conditions such as deadline and nonce must satisfy the specification. A valid signature alone cannot authorize execution of an expired approval.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing signature validity from permit deadlines

questions.question: When a timelock expires, the locked bitcoin is automatically sent to the recipient without a separate valid spending transaction.
questions.explanation: A timelock only defines when spending can become valid. Even after time passes, a transaction satisfying the spending conditions, including signatures, is required.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing timelocks from automatic payments

questions.question: Narrowing a concentrated-liquidity range necessarily produces a higher total return along every market path, regardless of potential capital-efficiency gains.
questions.explanation: A narrower range can improve efficiency while active, but the price can leave it more easily. Fee opportunities and changes in asset composition depend on the market path.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding the risks and efficiency of narrow liquidity ranges

questions.question: Even after earning trading fees, an AMM liquidity provider can finish with less value than simply holding the same initial assets.
questions.explanation: Fee income does not always offset relative losses from changes in asset composition. Overall performance must include the benchmark and all income and costs.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing fee income from overall performance

questions.question: The actual time for a Bitcoin transaction to reach a target number of confirmations can be predicted exactly by multiplying the block count by a fixed interval.
questions.explanation: Block intervals vary probabilistically, and the wait for initial transaction inclusion also varies. An average interval does not guarantee an exact completion time.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding uncertainty in confirmations and completion time

questions.question: Because eth_call does not charge on-chain gas fees, the called contract cannot revert.
questions.explanation: eth_call still executes code under EVM rules. Failed conditions or reverts can be returned independently of whether an on-chain query fee is charged.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing free queries from execution errors

questions.question: An SPV wallet's requests to an external node for relevant transaction information can reveal clues about the user's addresses or transactions of interest.
questions.explanation: Lightweight verification requires receiving data from external nodes. Request structure can let the node infer relevant transactions, so privacy needs separate consideration.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding privacy in lightweight-wallet requests

questions.question: A client authenticated as a Fabric network participant can change state without separately meeting any chaincode endorsement policy.
questions.explanation: Eligibility to participate differs from endorsement requirements for a particular transaction. Transactions from authenticated clients must still satisfy the relevant policy and commit validation.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing network membership from transaction endorsement

questions.question: ERC-721 requires tokenIds to be issued as consecutive integers increasing one by one from 1.
questions.explanation: A tokenId is a uint256 identifier and is not required to be consecutive. Implementations may use nonconsecutive identifiers or other generation rules.
questions.learningObjective: Correcting misconceptions about consecutive ERC-721 tokenIds

questions.question: Keeping all three private keys of a 2-of-3 wallet in the same backup on one device automatically creates three independent defenses against compromise of that device.
questions.explanation: Compromise of a shared device or backup can expose multiple keys simultaneously. Signature thresholds and independent storage environments must be designed separately.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding independence in multisignature key storage

questions.question: ERC-2612 nonces(owner) must always equal the Ethereum account's ordinary transaction nonce.
questions.explanation: A permit nonce is maintained by the token contract to prevent replay of signed approvals. It is a counter separate from the account transaction nonce.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing permit nonces from transaction nonces

questions.question: An ordinary CID string must include a file's creation time, so sorting CIDs always identifies the latest version.
questions.explanation: A CID identifies content; it is not a general sequence number ordered by creation time. Tracking the latest version requires separate naming or version information.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing CIDs from version timestamps

questions.question: Under the ERC-721 specification, ownerOf must fail for an invalid tokenId rather than treating it as a normal ownership query.
questions.explanation: An arbitrary owner must not be returned for an invalid NFT, including a nonexistent one. The specification requires invalid NFT queries to fail.
questions.learningObjective: Querying ownership of invalid NFTs

questions.question: Without an additional condition check, a payable function can accept a call that sends 0 ETH.
questions.explanation: payable permits calls carrying ETH. Requiring a strictly positive amount needs a separate condition on msg.value.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing payable from a minimum payment amount

questions.question: For an online device to broadcast a transaction signed by an offline wallet, the private key used for signing must also be sent to the online device.
questions.explanation: The online device only needs the fully signed transaction. Separating signature creation from broadcasting allows the private key to remain offline.
questions.learningObjective: Broadcasting the result of offline signing

questions.question: ERC-1155 balanceOfBatch can query multiple IDs for only one owner address in a single call.
questions.explanation: balanceOfBatch queries corresponding pairs from owner and ID arrays. One call can also include balance queries for different owners.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding the scope of ERC-1155 batch balance queries

questions.question: A Solidity pure function may freely read block environment values such as block.timestamp as long as it does not modify state.
questions.explanation: pure also restricts state-related reads. Reading environment values such as block.timestamp is not ordinarily allowed in a pure function.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding pure functions and block-context reads

questions.question: Even if a transaction reverts at the top level, events emitted earlier during its execution remain permanently as successful logs.
questions.explanation: A top-level revert cancels the execution's state changes and logs. Distinguish traces of execution from logs in the confirmed receipt.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding atomic rollback of execution and logs

questions.question: Bitcoin consensus rules fix the basic transaction fee at a constant percentage of the amount sent.
questions.explanation: An ordinary transaction's fee is the difference between total inputs and outputs. Transaction size and demand for block space matter; the fee is not a fixed percentage of the payment amount.
questions.learningObjective: Correcting the amount-proportional fee misconception

questions.question: The core ERC-1155 interface alone automatically enumerates every tokenId an owner holds, without separate event indexing.
questions.explanation: Balance queries operate on specified IDs. Discovering all IDs is not automatically part of the core interface, so indexing or another mechanism must be considered.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding the limits of core ERC-1155 enumeration

questions.question: The ERC-20 specification treats a zero-amount transfer as a normal transfer and requires it to emit a Transfer event.
questions.explanation: The specification does not allow standard event behavior to be omitted solely because the amount is zero. Indexers should not judge an event's validity from its amount alone.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding events for zero-value ERC-20 transfers

questions.question: A recovery phrase without a BIP-39 passphrase is encrypted into words, so publishing it in full does not expose spending authority.
questions.explanation: A recovery phrase is secret information used to reproduce a seed. Without an additional passphrase, someone who knows the phrase can recover the same keys.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding exposure of recovery phrases without a passphrase

questions.question: A state channel can provide an on-chain closing procedure using the latest valid state and a dispute deadline in case a counterparty refuses to cooperate.
questions.explanation: Channels normally use off-chain agreement but can be designed to force settlement through an L1 contract during disputes. Check monitoring and deadline-response requirements.
questions.learningObjective: Handling noncooperation in state channels

questions.question: eth_getTransactionCount is an RPC that returns the number of incoming deposit transactions received by an address.
questions.explanation: This RPC queries an account counter related to transactions sent by the account at the specified state. It does not count incoming deposits.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding the transaction-count RPC

questions.question: In a state channel operated by agreement among existing participants, a new participant can always freely join and change state without existing participants' consent or reconfiguring the channel.
questions.explanation: Channel permissions and update validity depend on the defined participant set and signature conditions. Changing participants requires the protocol's separate procedure.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding state-channel participant sets

questions.question: Even after wallet keys are recovered from a backup, displaying balances and transaction history may require querying or scanning blockchain data again.
questions.explanation: Keys reproduce spending authority, not the latest transaction ledger itself. The wallet finds chain data associated with its addresses to reconstruct the current state.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing key recovery from transaction-history recovery

questions.question: If many oracle nodes all use the same single external API, having enough nodes means the source data no longer has a single point of failure.
questions.explanation: Even many delivery nodes can share the effects of an error or outage if they rely on one data source. Evaluate node diversity and source-data diversity separately.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing oracle-node counts from source diversity

questions.question: If eth_getTransactionReceipt returns null, the transaction has conclusively been deemed permanently invalid under consensus rules.
questions.explanation: A receipt may be unavailable because a transaction has not yet entered a block or the queried node does not know it. null alone cannot establish permanent invalidity.
questions.learningObjective: Interpreting a null transaction receipt

questions.question: Even if code can be moved to an EVM-compatible rollup, the original chain's contract addresses, token liquidity, and stored state are not all automatically copied.
questions.explanation: Execution compatibility helps with deployment and tool reuse. Network-specific deployment addresses, state, and asset or liquidity connections require separate work.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing EVM compatibility from application-state migration

questions.question: An indexed string parameter in an ordinary ABI event always stores the original string directly in the topic, allowing it to be read without reversing a hash.
questions.explanation: For an indexed dynamic value, the topic stores a hash of the prescribed encoding. If the original content is needed, consider separate non-indexed data or another method.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding how dynamic indexed values appear in logs

questions.question: Spending a P2SH output requires both a matching hash for the supplied redeem script and satisfaction of that script's spending conditions.
questions.explanation: The hash match confirms that the originally specified script was supplied. Its actual spending conditions, such as signatures, must also be satisfied.
questions.learningObjective: Validating scripts when spending P2SH outputs

questions.question: Two ordinary contracts at different addresses do not automatically share storage just because they declare state variables with the same name.
questions.explanation: An ordinary contract's state belongs to its address-specific context. Shared storage or proxy execution requires a separate explicit structure.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding independent per-contract storage

questions.question: With the same CID format and hash method, doubling a file's size necessarily doubles the CID string's length.
questions.explanation: A CID represents a content structure and hash. It does not contain the whole file as a string, so its length is not proportional to file size.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguishing file size from CID length

questions.question: If an ERC-20 allowance is 40, successfully calling the standard approve(spender, 10) makes the new allowance 50.
questions.explanation: approve overwrites the allowance with the specified value instead of adding to it. The new allowance in this example is 10.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding how repeated approve calls overwrite allowance

questions.question: Other things being equal, changing only a Solidity function's return type necessarily changes its ABI function selector.
questions.explanation: Return types are not part of the signature used to calculate a function selector. The selector is based on the function name and input parameter types.
questions.learningObjective: Understanding why return types are excluded from function selectors

questions.question: Pinning the same content with several independent operators can improve availability if one provider goes offline.
questions.explanation: Replicated storage reduces the effect of one provider's outage. Actual maintenance of copies and network access are still required, so it is not an unconditional permanence guarantee.
